To ensure that this conditioning transfers to the combined Gauss–Newton matrix, we need a compatibility condition describing how the PDE term acts on directions that are poorly constrained (or unconstrained) by the data tangent features. In particular, we rule out nearly-flat PDE curvature on the data-orthogonal subspace and control the coupling between data-visible and data-invisible directions. This the object of Assumption B.1 that we now introduce.

In what follows, we will let, for any θ∈ℝp\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, Pθ∈ℝp×pP_{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p} denote the projection matrix onto the range of Gdata​(θ)G_{\mathrm{data}}(\theta), and I∈ℝp×pI\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p} the identity. For x∈ℝpx\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and A∈ℝp×pA\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}, we will also slightly abuse notation and respectively denote by ‖x‖:=x12+…+xp2\|x\|:=\sqrt{x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+x_{p}^{2}} and ‖A‖:=supv∈ℝp:‖v‖=1‖A​v‖\|A\|:=\sup_{v\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:\|v\|=1}\|Av\| their Euclidean and operator norm.

Assumption B.1.

Fix a set 𝒮⊂B​(θ0,R)\mathcal{S}\subset B(\theta_{0},R). There exist constants δ′,μ⟂>0\delta^{\prime},\mu_{\perp}>0 and ρ≥0\rho\geq 0, such that with probability at least 1−δ′1-\delta^{\prime} over the initialization θ0\theta_{0} and the random sampling of the collocation, boundary and supervised data points, the following holds for every θ∈𝒮\theta\in\mathcal{S}:

  • •

    λmin+​((I−Pθ)​GPDE​(θ)​(I−Pθ))≥μ⟂\displaystyle\lambda_{\min}^{+}\bigl((I-P_{\theta})G_{\mathrm{PDE}}(\theta)(I-P_{\theta})\bigr)\geq\mu_{\perp}, (B.20)

  • •

    ‖Pθ​GPDE​(θ)​(I−Pθ)‖≤ρ\displaystyle\left\|P_{\theta}G_{\mathrm{PDE}}(\theta)(I-P_{\theta})\right\|\leq\rho. (B.21)

Remark B.4.

If the supervised data is not random (e.g., coarse finite element grid), one can formulate Assumption B.1 in a completely analogous manner and reach the same conclusion.

Assumption B.1 allows to bound from below the smallest eigenvalue of Gλ​(θ)G_{\lambda}(\theta) on 𝒮\mathcal{S} by an explicit quantity γ​(λ)\gamma(\lambda), as we will now establish.

Proposition B.5.

Assume that the conditions of Proposition B.3 are satisfied with radius R>0R>0 and confidence level δinit\delta_{\mathrm{init}}, and let 𝒮⊂B​(θ0,R)\mathcal{S}\subset B(\theta_{0},R) be a set on the corresponding initialization event. Assume also that Assumption B.1 holds on 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Then, with probability 1−δinit−δ′≡1−δ1-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}-\delta^{\prime}\equiv 1-\delta we have for every λ>0\lambda>0 and θ∈𝒮\theta\in\mathcal{S},

λmin+​(Gλ​(θ))≥γ​(λ),\lambda_{\min}^{+}\bigl(G_{\lambda}(\theta)\bigr)\geq\gamma(\lambda), (B.22)

where

γ​(λ)≔(λ​μdata+μ⟂)−(λ​μdata−μ⟂)2+4​ρ22.\gamma(\lambda)\coloneqq\frac{(\lambda\mu_{\mathrm{data}}+\mu_{\perp})-\sqrt{(\lambda\mu_{\mathrm{data}}-\mu_{\perp})^{2}+4\rho^{2}}}{2}.

In particular, if ρ2<λ​μdata​μ⟂\rho^{2}<\lambda\mu_{\mathrm{data}}\mu_{\perp}, then γ​(λ)>0\gamma(\lambda)>0 uniformly over θ∈𝒮\theta\in\mathcal{S}.

Proof.

Fix θ∈𝒮\theta\in\mathcal{S}. Decompose any v∈ℝpv\in\mathbb{R}^{p} as v=v1+v2v=v_{1}+v_{2} with v1=Pθ​vv_{1}=P_{\theta}v and v2=(I−Pθ)​vv_{2}=(I-P_{\theta})v. Using Range⁡(Pθ)=Range⁡(Gdata​(θ))\operatorname{Range}(P_{\theta})=\operatorname{Range}(G_{\mathrm{data}}(\theta)) and (B.19),

v⊤​(λ​Gdata​(θ))​v=λ​v1⊤​Gdata​(θ)​v1≥λ​μdata​∥v1∥2.v^{\top}(\lambda G_{\mathrm{data}}(\theta))v=\lambda v_{1}^{\top}G_{\mathrm{data}}(\theta)v_{1}\geq\lambda\mu_{\mathrm{data}}\lVert v_{1}\rVert^{2}.

Similarly, by (• ‣ B.1), for v2v_{2} orthogonal to the kernel of (I−Pθ)​GPDE​(θ)​(I−Pθ)(I-P_{\theta})G_{\mathrm{PDE}}(\theta)(I-P_{\theta}), we have

v2⊤​GPDE​(θ)​v2=v⊤​(I−Pθ)​GPDE​(θ)​(I−Pθ)​v≥μ⟂​∥v2∥2.v_{2}^{\top}G_{\mathrm{PDE}}(\theta)v_{2}=v^{\top}(I-P_{\theta})G_{\mathrm{PDE}}(\theta)(I-P_{\theta})v\geq\mu_{\perp}\lVert v_{2}\rVert^{2}.

For the cross term, by (• ‣ B.1),

2​v1⊤​GPDE​(θ)​v2≥−2​∥Pθ​GPDE​(θ)​(I−Pθ)∥​∥v1∥​∥v2∥≥−2​ρ​∥v1∥​∥v2∥.2v_{1}^{\top}G_{\mathrm{PDE}}(\theta)v_{2}\geq-2\lVert P_{\theta}G_{\mathrm{PDE}}(\theta)(I-P_{\theta})\rVert\,\lVert v_{1}\rVert\,\lVert v_{2}\rVert\geq-2\rho\,\lVert v_{1}\rVert\,\lVert v_{2}\rVert.

Putting these together,

v⊤​Gλ​(θ)​v≥[∥v1∥∥v2∥]⊤​[λ​μdata−ρ−ρμ⟂]​[∥v1∥∥v2∥].v^{\top}G_{\lambda}(\theta)v\geq\begin{bmatrix}\lVert v_{1}\rVert\\ \lVert v_{2}\rVert\end{bmatrix}^{\!\top}\begin{bmatrix}\lambda\mu_{\mathrm{data}}&-\rho\\ -\rho&\mu_{\perp}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\lVert v_{1}\rVert\\ \lVert v_{2}\rVert\end{bmatrix}.

Minimizing over ∥v∥=1\lVert v\rVert=1 yields the smallest eigenvalue of the displayed 2×22\times 2 matrix, which equals γ​(λ)\gamma(\lambda). By the variational formulation of the smallest non-zero eigenvalue, the claimed lower bound on λmin+​(Gλ​(θ))\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\lambda}(\theta)) follows. ∎

Remark B.6.

Note that although we did not include it for simplicity, the boundary loss term has the same least-squares form as a supervised data term, so its Gauss–Newton contribution Gbc​(θ)G_{\mathrm{bc}}(\theta) is positive semidefinite and can be handled in an analogous manner. More specifically, in Proposition B.5 and Theorem B.9 we can include the boundary term while assuming that Gbc​(θ)G_{\mathrm{bc}}(\theta) satisfies Assumption B.1 as well. The analogous conclusion then follows by mirroring the current argument.

B.5 PL constant, condition number, and gradient descent

We now translate the spectral bounds from Proposition B.5 into a Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL\mathrm{PL}) constant and condition number for LλL_{\lambda}, and derive implications for gradient descent.

PL inequality and PL-based condition number

Let 𝒮⊂ℝp\mathcal{S}\subset\mathbb{R}^{p} be a set containing θλ⋆\theta_{\lambda}^{\star}. We say that LλL_{\lambda} satisfies a PL∗ inequality with constant μλ>0\mu_{\lambda}>0 on 𝒮\mathcal{S} if

‖∇Lλ​(θ)‖222​μλ≥Lλ​(θ)−Lλ​(θλ⋆),∀θ∈𝒮.\frac{\bigl\|\nabla L_{\lambda}(\theta)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}}{2\mu_{\lambda}}\;\geq\;L_{\lambda}(\theta)-L_{\lambda}(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star}),\quad\forall\,\theta\in\mathcal{S}. (B.23)

Let βLλ\beta_{L_{\lambda}} denote a smoothness constant on 𝒮\mathcal{S}, i.e. an upper bound on the operator norm of the Hessian,

βLλ≥supθ∈𝒮‖HLλ​(θ)‖.\beta_{L_{\lambda}}\;\geq\;\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal{S}}\bigl\|H_{L_{\lambda}}(\theta)\bigr\|.

The PL\mathrm{PL}-based condition number of LλL_{\lambda} on 𝒮\mathcal{S} is then defined by

κLλ​(𝒮):=βLλμλ.\kappa_{L_{\lambda}}(\mathcal{S}):=\frac{\beta_{L_{\lambda}}}{\mu_{\lambda}}. (B.24)

We will use the following Lemma, which is nothing more than (Liu et al., 2022, Theorem 1) reformulated in our setup.

Lemma B.7.

Let L​(θ)=12​‖F​(θ)‖22L(\theta)=\tfrac{1}{2}\|F(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}, where F:ℝp→ℝnF:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} is differentiable on a set 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Suppose there exists θ⋆∈𝒮\theta^{\star}\in\mathcal{S} with F​(θ⋆)=0F(\theta^{\star})=0. Define the sample tangent kernel KF​(θ):=JF​(θ)​JF​(θ)⊤K_{F}(\theta):=J_{F}(\theta)\,J_{F}(\theta)^{\top}. If there exists μ>0\mu>0 such that λmin​(KF​(θ))≥μ\lambda_{\min}(K_{F}(\theta))\geq\mu holds for every θ∈𝒮\theta\in\mathcal{S}, then LL satisfies the PL∗ inequality on 𝒮\mathcal{S} with constant μ\mu.

Proof.

For θ∈𝒮\theta\in\mathcal{S}, ∇L​(θ)=JF​(θ)⊤​F​(θ)\nabla L(\theta)=J_{F}(\theta)^{\top}F(\theta), hence ‖∇L​(θ)‖22=F​(θ)⊤​KF​(θ)​F​(θ)\|\nabla L(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}=F(\theta)^{\top}K_{F}(\theta)F(\theta). The assumed bound gives ‖∇L​(θ)‖22≥μ​‖F​(θ)‖22=2​μ​L​(θ)\|\nabla L(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}\geq\mu\|F(\theta)\|_{2}^{2}=2\mu L(\theta). Since L​(θ⋆)=0L(\theta^{\star})=0, this is the claimed PL∗ inequality. ∎

From basic linear algebra, we have the following relationship between the non-zero spectrum of KFK_{F} and that of GFG_{F}:

Lemma B.8.

Let F:ℝp→ℝnF:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} be differentiable at θ\theta, with Jacobian JF​(θ)J_{F}(\theta). Define GF​(θ):=JF​(θ)⊤​JF​(θ)G_{F}(\theta):=J_{F}(\theta)^{\top}J_{F}(\theta) and KF​(θ):=JF​(θ)​JF​(θ)⊤K_{F}(\theta):=J_{F}(\theta)J_{F}(\theta)^{\top}. Then GF​(θ)G_{F}(\theta) and KF​(θ)K_{F}(\theta) have the same nonzero eigenvalues. If JF​(θ)J_{F}(\theta) has full row rank, then KF​(θ)K_{F}(\theta) is positive definite and λmin​(KF​(θ))=λmin+​(GF​(θ))\lambda_{\min}\bigl(K_{F}(\theta)\bigr)=\lambda_{\min}^{+}\bigl(G_{F}(\theta)\bigr).

Bounding the PL constant and condition number

Lemma B.7 applied to FλF_{\lambda} shows that it suffices to control the smallest eigenvalue of the stacked sample kernel KFλ​(θ)K_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta) on 𝒮\mathcal{S} to obtain a PL∗ inequality. Lemma B.8 on the other hand shows that this smallest eigenvalue is equal to the non-zero such eigenvalue of GλG_{\lambda}. Combining these facts with Proposition B.5, which gives a lower bound on λmin+​(Gλ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}(G_{\lambda}) yields the following uniform bound on the PL-based condition number, which is our main result.

Theorem B.9.

Fix confidence levels δinit∈(0,1)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}\in(0,1) and δ′∈(0,1)\delta^{\prime}\in(0,1). Choose the width mm so that Proposition B.3 holds with δ=δinit\delta=\delta_{\mathrm{init}}, and let 𝒮⊂B​(θ0,R)\mathcal{S}\subset B(\theta_{0},R) be any set containing a global minimizer θλ⋆\theta_{\lambda}^{\star} of LλL_{\lambda} satisfying Fλ​(θλ⋆)=0F_{\lambda}(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star})=0. Assume that Assumption B.1 holds on 𝒮\mathcal{S} with confidence parameter δ′\delta^{\prime}, and let γ​(λ)\gamma(\lambda) be as in Proposition B.5.

Assume that JFλJ_{F_{\lambda}} is Lipschitz on 𝒮\mathcal{S} with constant LJ>0L_{J}>0. Assume also that JFλ​(θλ⋆)J_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star}) has full row rank, and define

sλ:=σmin​(JFλ​(θλ⋆)),rλ:=sλ2​LJ, and ​𝒮λ:=𝒮∩B​(θλ⋆,rλ).s_{\lambda}:=\sigma_{\min}\bigl(J_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star})\bigr),\ \ r_{\lambda}:=\frac{s_{\lambda}}{2L_{J}},\ \text{ and }\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}:=\mathcal{S}\cap B(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star},r_{\lambda}).

Lastly, assume that there exist finite constants BF,BJ>0B_{F},B_{J}>0 such that supθ∈𝒮λ‖Fλ​(θ)‖2≤BF\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}}\|F_{\lambda}(\theta)\|_{2}\leq B_{F} and supθ∈𝒮λ‖JFλ​(θ)‖≤BJ\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}}\|J_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta)\|\leq B_{J}.

Then, with probability at least 1−δinit−δ′≡1−δ1-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}-\delta^{\prime}\equiv 1-\delta, the loss LλL_{\lambda} satisfies a PL∗\mathrm{PL}^{\ast} inequality on 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} with constant μλ\mu_{\lambda} obeying

μλ≥γ​(λ).\mu_{\lambda}\geq\gamma(\lambda). (B.25)

Moreover, LλL_{\lambda} is βLλ\beta_{L_{\lambda}}-smooth on 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} with βLλ≤BJ2+LJ​BF\beta_{L_{\lambda}}\leq B_{J}^{2}+L_{J}B_{F}, and its PL\mathrm{PL}-based condition number on 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} satisfies

κLλ​(𝒮λ)≤BJ2+LJ​BFγ​(λ).\kappa_{L_{\lambda}}(\mathcal{S}_{\lambda})\leq\frac{B_{J}^{2}+L_{J}B_{F}}{\gamma(\lambda)}. (B.26)
Proof.

Work on the intersection of the initialization event from Proposition B.3 with δ=δinit\delta=\delta_{\mathrm{init}} and the event in Assumption B.1 on 𝒮\mathcal{S}. This intersection event has probability at least 1−δinit−δ′1-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}-\delta^{\prime}, and on it Proposition B.5 gives λmin+​(Gλ​(θ))≥γ​(λ)\lambda_{\min}^{+}\bigl(G_{\lambda}(\theta)\bigr)\geq\gamma(\lambda) for every θ∈𝒮\theta\in\mathcal{S}.

We next propagate full row rank from θλ⋆\theta_{\lambda}^{\star} to 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}. For any θ∈𝒮λ\theta\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}, Weyl’s inequalities for singular value perturbations (Horn and Johnson, 2012) yields

σmin​(JFλ​(θ))≥σmin​(JFλ​(θλ⋆))−‖JFλ​(θ)−JFλ​(θλ⋆)‖≥sλ−LJ​‖θ−θλ⋆‖≥sλ2.\sigma_{\min}\bigl(J_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta)\bigr)\geq\sigma_{\min}\bigl(J_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star})\bigr)-\bigl\|J_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta)-J_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star})\bigr\|\geq s_{\lambda}-L_{J}\|\theta-\theta_{\lambda}^{\star}\|\geq\frac{s_{\lambda}}{2}.

Therefore JFλ​(θ)J_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta) has full row rank for every θ∈𝒮λ\theta\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}. Lemma B.8 then implies that λmin​(KFλ​(θ))=λmin+​(Gλ​(θ))\lambda_{\min}\bigl(K_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta)\bigr)=\lambda_{\min}^{+}\bigl(G_{\lambda}(\theta)\bigr) holds for every θ∈𝒮λ\theta\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}, hence λmin​(KFλ​(θ))≥γ​(λ)\lambda_{\min}\bigl(K_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta)\bigr)\geq\gamma(\lambda) on 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}. Applying Lemma B.7 to Lλ​(θ)=12​‖Fλ​(θ)‖22L_{\lambda}(\theta)=\tfrac{1}{2}\|F_{\lambda}(\theta)\|_{2}^{2} and Fλ​(θλ⋆)=0F_{\lambda}(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star})=0 yields the PL∗\mathrm{PL}^{\ast} inequality on 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} with constant μλ≥γ​(λ),\mu_{\lambda}\geq\gamma(\lambda), which is (B.25).

For smoothness on 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}, use ∇Lλ​(θ)=JFλ​(θ)⊤​Fλ​(θ)\nabla L_{\lambda}(\theta)=J_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta)^{\top}F_{\lambda}(\theta) to write, for θ,θ′∈𝒮λ\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda},

∇Lλ​(θ)−∇Lλ​(θ′)=(JFλ​(θ)−JFλ​(θ′))⊤​Fλ​(θ)+JFλ​(θ′)⊤​(Fλ​(θ)−Fλ​(θ′)).\nabla L_{\lambda}(\theta)-\nabla L_{\lambda}(\theta^{\prime})=\bigl(J_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta)-J_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta^{\prime})\bigr)^{\top}F_{\lambda}(\theta)+J_{F_{\lambda}}(\theta^{\prime})^{\top}\bigl(F_{\lambda}(\theta)-F_{\lambda}(\theta^{\prime})\bigr).

The first term is bounded by LJ​‖θ−θ′‖​‖Fλ​(θ)‖2≤LJ​BF​‖θ−θ′‖L_{J}\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|\,\|F_{\lambda}(\theta)\|_{2}\leq L_{J}B_{F}\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|. For the second term, the mean value inequality gives ‖Fλ​(θ)−Fλ​(θ′)‖2≤supξ∈𝒮λ‖JFλ​(ξ)‖​‖θ−θ′‖≤BJ​‖θ−θ′‖\|F_{\lambda}(\theta)-F_{\lambda}(\theta^{\prime})\|_{2}\leq\sup_{\xi\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}}\|J_{F_{\lambda}}(\xi)\|\,\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|\leq B_{J}\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|, hence the second term is bounded by BJ2​‖θ−θ′‖B_{J}^{2}\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|. Altogether,

‖∇Lλ​(θ)−∇Lλ​(θ′)‖≤(BJ2+LJ​BF)​‖θ−θ′‖​ for all ​θ,θ′∈𝒮λ.\|\nabla L_{\lambda}(\theta)-\nabla L_{\lambda}(\theta^{\prime})\|\leq(B_{J}^{2}+L_{J}B_{F})\,\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|\text{ for all }\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}.

Therefore LλL_{\lambda} is βLλ\beta_{L_{\lambda}}-smooth on 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda} with βLλ≤BJ2+LJ​BF\beta_{L_{\lambda}}\leq B_{J}^{2}+L_{J}B_{F}. Combining this with (B.25) and the definition (B.24) yields (B.26). ∎

In the PDE-only case λ=0\lambda=0, Proposition B.2 gives μ0≍nres−α\mu_{0}\asymp n_{\mathrm{res}}^{-\alpha}, so the PL\mathrm{PL} based condition number κL0​(𝒮)\kappa_{L_{0}}(\mathcal{S}) grows like nresαn_{\mathrm{res}}^{\alpha}. In contrast, (B.25)–(B.26) show that if λ>ρ2/(μdata​μ⟂)\lambda>\rho^{2}/(\mu_{\mathrm{data}}\mu_{\perp}) is fixed independently of nresn_{\mathrm{res}}, then μλ\mu_{\lambda} is bounded away from zero and κLλ​(𝒮)\kappa_{L_{\lambda}}(\mathcal{S}) remains bounded as more residual points are added.

Gradient descent convergence under uniform conditioning

Consider gradient descent on LλL_{\lambda},

θk+1=θk−η​∇Lλ​(θk),\theta_{k+1}=\theta_{k}-\eta\,\nabla L_{\lambda}(\theta_{k}),

with a fixed step size η∈(0,1/βLλ]\eta\in(0,1/\beta_{L_{\lambda}}], and assume that the iterates stay in 𝒮λ\mathcal{S}_{\lambda}. Under the setting of Theorem B.9, the result of Liu et al. (2022, Theorem 6) gives

Lλ​(θk+1)−Lλ​(θλ⋆)≤(1−η​μλ)​(Lλ​(θk)−Lλ​(θλ⋆)).L_{\lambda}(\theta_{k+1})-L_{\lambda}(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star})\;\leq\;\bigl(1-\eta\mu_{\lambda}\bigr)\,\bigl(L_{\lambda}(\theta_{k})-L_{\lambda}(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star})\bigr).

Choosing η=1/βLλ\eta=1/\beta_{L_{\lambda}} and using (B.24)–(B.26), we obtain

Lλ​(θk+1)−Lλ​(θλ⋆)≤(1−1κLλ​(𝒮))​(Lλ​(θk)−Lλ​(θλ⋆)).L_{\lambda}(\theta_{k+1})-L_{\lambda}(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star})\;\leq\;\biggl(1-\frac{1}{\kappa_{L_{\lambda}}(\mathcal{S})}\biggr)\,\bigl(L_{\lambda}(\theta_{k})-L_{\lambda}(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star})\bigr).

Thus the number of iterations required to reach Lλ​(θk)−Lλ​(θλ⋆)≤εL_{\lambda}(\theta_{k})-L_{\lambda}(\theta_{\lambda}^{\star})\leq\varepsilon is

𝒪​(κLλ​(𝒮)​log⁡(1/ε)).\mathcal{O}\bigl(\kappa_{L_{\lambda}}(\mathcal{S})\,\log(1/\varepsilon)\bigr).

In particular, in virtue of Theorem B.9, we see that this iteration complexity is bounded uniformly in nresn_{\mathrm{res}} when λ>0\lambda>0 is fixed.

Appendix C Monte Carlo Feynman–Kac label noise

This section provides the probabilistic error analysis for the Monte Carlo Feynman–Kac estimator used to construct the FK supervision labels in ℛFK​-​PINN\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{FK\text{-}PINN}}. Our goal is to justify Proposition 6.1 in the main text, namely that each FK datum can be written as a noisy point evaluation of the true solution u⋆u^{\star} with sub-exponential noise whose parameters do not depend on the number of FK points.

Throughout this section, we fix a spatial point x∈Ωx\in\Omega and study the error of the Monte Carlo Feynman–Kac estimator at this point. All constants may depend on the model data (domain, coefficients, source and boundary terms) and, when a truncation horizon TmaxT_{\max} is present, on TmaxT_{\max}. They do not depend on the Monte Carlo sample size NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}} and they do not depend on the time step Δ​t\Delta t once Δ​t\Delta t is restricted to be smaller than a suitable threshold.

C.1 Setting and numerical scheme

We recall the diffusion setting that underlies the Feynman–Kac representation.

Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a bounded domain with C2C^{2} boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega. Let b:ℝd→ℝdb:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} and σ:ℝd→ℝd×m\sigma:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times m} be globally Lipschitz functions. We assume that σ\sigma is uniformly elliptic, i.e. there exist constants 0<λ¯≤λ¯<∞0<\underline{\lambda}\leq\overline{\lambda}<\infty such that

λ¯​|v|2≤v⊤​(σ​σ⊤)​(x)​v≤λ¯​|v|2, for all ​x,v∈ℝd.\underline{\lambda}\,\lvert v\rvert^{2}\;\leq\;v^{\top}(\sigma\sigma^{\top})(x)v\;\leq\;\overline{\lambda}\,\lvert v\rvert^{2},\ \text{ for all }x,v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Let (Wt)t≥0(W_{t})_{t\geq 0} be an mm-dimensional Brownian motion on some filtered probability space (Ω,ℱ,(ℱt)t≥0,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\geq 0},\mathbb{P}).

The diffusion process X=(Xt)t≥0X=(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} is the unique strong solution of

d​Xt=b​(Xt)​d​t+σ​(Xt)​d​Wt,X0=x∈Ω.dX_{t}=b(X_{t})\,dt+\sigma(X_{t})\,dW_{t},\quad X_{0}=x\in\Omega. (C.1)

We denote by

τ:=inf{t≥0:Xt∉Ω}\tau:=\inf\{t\geq 0:X_{t}\notin\Omega\}

the first exit time of the diffusion from Ω\Omega, and assume τ<∞\tau<\infty almost surely for all starting points x∈Ωx\in\Omega.

Let f:Ω¯→ℝf:\overline{\Omega}\to\mathbb{R}, g:∂Ω→ℝg:\partial\Omega\to\mathbb{R} and V:Ω¯→ℝV:\overline{\Omega}\to\mathbb{R} be bounded measurable functions. In the main text these correspond to the source term, boundary data and zeroth-order potential of the elliptic boundary value problem. The associated (continuous-time) Feynman–Kac payoff is

Y:=∫0τexp⁡(−∫0tV​(Xs)​𝑑s)​f​(Xt)​𝑑t+exp⁡(−∫0τV​(Xs)​𝑑s)​g​(Xτ).Y:=\int_{0}^{\tau}\exp\Bigl(-\int_{0}^{t}V(X_{s})\,ds\Bigr)\,f(X_{t})\,dt\;+\;\exp\Bigl(-\int_{0}^{\tau}V(X_{s})\,ds\Bigr)\,g(X_{\tau}). (C.2)

Under standard regularity and well-posedness assumptions (Evans, 2022), the elliptic boundary value problem admits a unique solution u⋆u^{\star}, and one has the Feynman–Kac representation

u⋆​(x)=𝔼x​[Y],u^{\star}(x)\;=\;\mathbb{E}^{x}[Y],

where 𝔼x\mathbb{E}^{x} denotes expectation for the diffusion (C.1) started at X0=xX_{0}=x.

For the numerical approximation we fix a time step Δ​t>0\Delta t>0 and define the Euler–Maruyama scheme (XkΔ​t)k∈ℕ0(X_{k}^{\Delta t})_{k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}} by

X0Δ​t=x,Xk+1Δ​t=XkΔ​t+b​(XkΔ​t)​Δ​t+σ​(XkΔ​t)​Δ​Wk,X_{0}^{\Delta t}=x,\quad X_{k+1}^{\Delta t}=X_{k}^{\Delta t}+b(X_{k}^{\Delta t})\,\Delta t+\sigma(X_{k}^{\Delta t})\,\Delta W_{k}, (C.3)

where Δ​Wk:=W(k+1)​Δ​t−Wk​Δ​t\Delta W_{k}:=W_{(k+1)\Delta t}-W_{k\Delta t}. The corresponding discrete exit time is

τΔ​t:=inf{k​Δ​t:XkΔ​t∉Ω},\tau_{\Delta t}:=\inf\{k\Delta t:X_{k}^{\Delta t}\notin\Omega\}, (C.4)

with the convention inf∅=∞\inf\emptyset=\infty. Writing

NΔ​t:=inf{k∈ℕ0:XkΔ​t∉Ω},N_{\Delta t}:=\inf\{k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}:X_{k}^{\Delta t}\notin\Omega\},

we have τΔ​t=NΔ​t​Δ​t\tau_{\Delta t}=N_{\Delta t}\Delta t.

The discretized payoff functional is

YΔ​t:=∑k=0NΔ​t−1exp⁡(−Δ​t​∑j=0k−1V​(XjΔ​t))​f​(XkΔ​t)​Δ​t+exp⁡(−Δ​t​∑j=0NΔ​t−1V​(XjΔ​t))​g​(XNΔ​tΔ​t).Y^{\Delta t}:=\sum_{k=0}^{N_{\Delta t}-1}\exp\Bigl(-\Delta t\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}V(X_{j}^{\Delta t})\Bigr)f(X_{k}^{\Delta t})\,\Delta t\;+\;\exp\Bigl(-\Delta t\sum_{j=0}^{N_{\Delta t}-1}V(X_{j}^{\Delta t})\Bigr)g(X_{N_{\Delta t}}^{\Delta t}). (C.5)

The associated time-discretized value at xx is

uΔ​t​(x):=𝔼x​[YΔ​t].u_{\Delta t}(x):=\mathbb{E}^{x}[Y^{\Delta t}].

Given NMC∈ℕN_{\mathrm{MC}}\in\mathbb{N}, we consider i.i.d. copies (YΔ​t,(i))i=1NMC(Y^{\Delta t,(i)})_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{MC}}} of YΔ​tY^{\Delta t} and define the Monte Carlo estimator (for fixed xx and Δ​t\Delta t)

u^MC​(x):=1NMC​∑i=1NMCYΔ​t,(i).\widehat{u}^{\mathrm{MC}}(x):=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{MC}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{MC}}}Y^{\Delta t,(i)}. (C.6)

In practice Algorithm 1 simulates trajectories until they exit Ω\Omega or until a truncation horizon Tmax∈(0,∞]T_{\max}\in(0,\infty] is reached. For Tmax=∞T_{\max}=\infty this reduces to the infinite horizon estimator u^MC​(x)\widehat{u}^{\mathrm{MC}}(x) defined above. For a finite truncation horizon we set NT:=⌊Tmax/Δ​t⌋N_{T}:=\lfloor T_{\max}/\Delta t\rfloor and define the truncated discrete stopping index

κΔ​tTmax:=min⁡{NΔ​t,NT},\kappa_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}:=\min\{N_{\Delta t},N_{T}\},

together with the truncated payoff

YΔ​t,Tmax:=∑k=0κΔ​tTmax−1exp⁡(−Δ​t​∑j=0k−1V​(XjΔ​t))​f​(XkΔ​t)​Δ​t+exp⁡(−Δ​t​∑j=0κΔ​tTmax−1V​(XjΔ​t))​g​(XκΔ​tTmaxΔ​t).Y^{\Delta t,T_{\max}}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\kappa_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}-1}\exp\Bigl(-\Delta t\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}V(X_{j}^{\Delta t})\Bigr)f(X_{k}^{\Delta t})\,\Delta t\;+\;\exp\Bigl(-\Delta t\sum_{j=0}^{\kappa_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}-1}V(X_{j}^{\Delta t})\Bigr)g(X_{\kappa_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}}^{\Delta t}). (C.7)

We write uΔ​tTmax​(x):=𝔼x​[YΔ​t,Tmax]u_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}(x):=\mathbb{E}^{x}[Y^{\Delta t,T_{\max}}] for the corresponding truncated value. For Tmax=∞T_{\max}=\infty we adopt the convention YΔ​t,∞:=YΔ​tY^{\Delta t,\infty}:=Y^{\Delta t} and uΔ​t∞​(x):=uΔ​t​(x)u_{\Delta t}^{\infty}(x):=u_{\Delta t}(x) so that the notation covers both finite and infinite horizons. Our aim is to control the tails of FK estimators of the form u^MC​(x)\widehat{u}^{\mathrm{MC}}(x) and of their truncated counterparts, and hence show that the resulting FK labels behave like noisy point evaluations of u⋆u^{\star} with sub-exponential noise.

C.2 Exit time estimates and exponential moments

We first establish exponential moments for the continuous exit time τ\tau and the discrete exit time τΔ​t\tau_{\Delta t}. These are the key inputs for controlling the tails of the payoffs YY and YΔ​tY^{\Delta t} and hence the Monte Carlo error.

C.2.1 Continuous exit time

Theorem C.1 (Exponential moments of the continuous exit time).

Suppose that Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is a bounded C2C^{2} domain and that the diffusion XX defined by (C.1) has globally Lipschitz coefficients and is uniformly elliptic. Then there exist constants λc>0\lambda_{c}>0 and Cc<∞C_{c}<\infty such that

supy∈Ω¯𝔼y​[eλc​τ]≤Cc.\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{E}^{y}\big[e^{\lambda_{c}\tau}\big]\;\leq\;C_{c}.

In particular, the law of τ\tau has exponential tails uniformly over starting points y∈Ω¯y\in\overline{\Omega}.

Proof.

Under these assumptions, the generator ℒ\mathcal{L} of XX with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions on ∂Ω\partial\Omega admits a discrete spectrum with strictly positive first eigenvalue λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0 (Pinsky, 1995). The killed semigroup (PtΩ)t≥0(P_{t}^{\Omega})_{t\geq 0} therefore satisfies

∥PtΩ∥L∞​(Ω)→L∞​(Ω)≤C​e−λ1​t, for all ​t≥0\lVert P_{t}^{\Omega}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)\to L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq Ce^{-\lambda_{1}t},\ \text{ for all }t\geq 0

for some constant C<∞C<\infty. It follows that

supy∈Ω¯ℙy​(τ>t)=supy∈Ω¯PtΩ​𝟏​(y)≤C​e−λ1​t, for all ​t≥0.\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau>t)=\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}P_{t}^{\Omega}\mathbf{1}(y)\leq Ce^{-\lambda_{1}t},\ \text{ for all }t\geq 0.

Fix any λc∈(0,λ1)\lambda_{c}\in(0,\lambda_{1}). Then, integrating the tail bound,

𝔼y​[eλc​τ]=1+∫0∞λc​eλc​t​ℙy​(τ>t)​𝑑t≤1+C​λc​∫0∞e−(λ1−λc)​t​𝑑t<∞,\mathbb{E}^{y}\big[e^{\lambda_{c}\tau}\big]=1+\int_{0}^{\infty}\lambda_{c}e^{\lambda_{c}t}\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau>t)\,dt\leq 1+C\lambda_{c}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{c})t}\,dt<\infty,

with the bound uniform in y∈Ω¯y\in\overline{\Omega}. This proves the claim for a suitable constant CcC_{c}. ∎

C.2.2 Discrete exit time

We next recall moment estimates for the discrete exit time τΔ​t\tau_{\Delta t}. We rely on the results of Bouchard et al. (2017).

Theorem C.2 (Moments of continuous and discrete exit times).

Assume that Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is a bounded C2C^{2} domain with non-characteristic boundary, and that the coefficients b,σb,\sigma in (C.1) are globally Lipschitz and of linear growth. Let τ\tau be as above and τΔ​t\tau_{\Delta t} be defined by (C.4). Then, for each integer p≥1p\geq 1, there exist finite constants Cp<∞C_{p}<\infty and Δ​tp>0\Delta t_{p}>0 such that for all 0<Δ​t≤Δ​tp0<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{p},

supy∈Ω¯𝔼y​[τp]\displaystyle\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{E}^{y}[\tau^{p}] ≤Cp,\displaystyle\leq C_{p},
supy∈Ω¯𝔼y​[τΔ​tp]\displaystyle\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{E}^{y}[\tau_{\Delta t}^{p}] ≤Cp,\displaystyle\leq C_{p},
supy∈Ω¯𝔼y​[|τΔ​t−τ|p]\displaystyle\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{E}^{y}\big[\lvert\tau_{\Delta t}-\tau\rvert^{p}\big] ≤Cp​Δ​tp/2.\displaystyle\leq C_{p}\,\Delta t^{p/2}.
Proof.

This is a specialization of the main results in Bouchard et al. (2017). See in particular Theorems 3.1 there, specialized to globally Lipschitz coefficients and a bounded C2C^{2} domain. The non-characteristic boundary condition is implied by uniform ellipticity. Collecting the corresponding bounds yields the stated result. ∎

Combining Theorems C.1 and C.2, one can show that τΔ​t\tau_{\Delta t} admits exponential moments uniformly over Δ​t\Delta t small enough by a standard renewal argument. We sketch this in the next two lemmas.

Lemma C.3 (Uniform exit in finite time).

Under the standing assumptions, there exist constants T∗>0T_{\ast}>0 and p0∈(0,1)p_{0}\in(0,1) such that

infy∈Ω¯ℙy​(τ≤T∗)≥p0.\inf_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau\leq T_{\ast})\;\geq\;p_{0}.

Moreover, there exist Δ​t0>0\Delta t_{0}>0 and p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) such that for all 0<Δ​t≤Δ​t00<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0},

infy∈Ω¯ℙy​(τΔ​t≤T∗)≥p.\inf_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau_{\Delta t}\leq T_{\ast})\;\geq\;p.
Proof sketch.

For the continuous exit time, Theorem C.1 yields supy∈Ω¯ℙy​(τ>t)≤Cc​e−λc​t\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau>t)\leq C_{c}e^{-\lambda_{c}t}, hence, choosing T∗T_{\ast} large enough that Cc​e−λc​T∗≤1/2C_{c}e^{-\lambda_{c}T_{\ast}}\leq 1/2 gives

infy∈Ω¯ℙy(τ≤T∗)≥1/2=:p0.\inf_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau\leq T_{\ast})\geq 1/2=:p_{0}.

By Theorem C.2, for some p≥1p\geq 1 we have supy∈Ω¯𝔼y​[|τΔ​t−τ|p]→0​ as ​Δ​t→0\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{E}^{y}\big[|\tau_{\Delta t}-\tau|^{p}\big]\to 0\text{ as }\Delta t\to 0, hence, for any ε>0\varepsilon>0,

supy∈Ω¯ℙy​(|τΔ​t−τ|>ε)≤ε−p​supy𝔼y​[|τΔ​t−τ|p]→0,\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{P}^{y}\big(|\tau_{\Delta t}-\tau|>\varepsilon\big)\leq\varepsilon^{-p}\sup_{y}\mathbb{E}^{y}\big[|\tau_{\Delta t}-\tau|^{p}\big]\to 0,

so τΔ​t→τ\tau_{\Delta t}\to\tau in probability, uniformly in yy. Since the law of τ\tau has a density (see, e.g., Pinsky (1995)), we have ℙy​(τ=T∗)=0\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau=T_{\ast})=0 for all yy, and thus ℙy​(τΔ​t≤T∗)⟶ℙy​(τ≤T∗)\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau_{\Delta t}\leq T_{\ast})\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau\leq T_{\ast}) uniformly in y∈Ω¯y\in\overline{\Omega} as Δ​t→0\Delta t\to 0. Hence for Δ​t\Delta t small enough we still have

infy∈Ω¯ℙy(τΔ​t≤T∗)≥p0/2=:p∈(0,1).\inf_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau_{\Delta t}\leq T_{\ast})\geq p_{0}/2=:p\in(0,1).

∎

Proposition C.4 (Exponential moments of the discrete exit time).

Under the standing assumptions, there exist constants λd>0\lambda_{d}>0, Cd<∞C_{d}<\infty and Δ​t0>0\Delta t_{0}>0 such that

supy∈Ω¯, 0<Δ​t≤Δ​t0𝔼y​[eλd​τΔ​t]≤Cd.\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega},\,0<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}}\mathbb{E}^{y}\big[e^{\lambda_{d}\tau_{\Delta t}}\big]\;\leq\;C_{d}.
Proof sketch.

Let T∗>0T_{\ast}>0, p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) and Δ​t0>0\Delta t_{0}>0 be as in Lemma C.3. In particular, infyℙy​(τΔ​t≤T∗)≥p\inf_{y}\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau_{\Delta}t\leq T_{\ast})\geq p, so supyℙy​(τΔ​t>T∗)≤1−p\sup_{y}\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau_{\Delta}t>T_{\ast})\leq 1-p for all 0<Δ​t≤Δ​t00<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}.

Consider the continuous-time interpolation of the Euler scheme, which is a time-homogeneous Markov process. By the (strong) Markov property at times k​T∗kT_{\ast},

ℙy​(τΔ​t>(k+1)​T∗)=𝔼y​[𝟏{τΔ​t>k​T∗}​ℙXΔ​tk​T∗​(τΔ​t>T∗)]≤(1−p)​ℙy​(τΔ​t>k​T∗).\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau_{\Delta t}>(k+1)T_{\ast})=\mathbb{E}^{y}\big[\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{\Delta}t>kT_{\ast}\}}\mathbb{P}^{X^{\Delta}t_{kT_{\ast}}}(\tau_{\Delta}t>T_{\ast})\big]\leq(1-p)\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau_{\Delta}t>kT_{\ast}).

Iterating this inequality gives supy∈Ω¯ℙy​(τΔ​t>k​T∗)≤(1−p)k\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau_{\Delta t}>kT_{\ast})\leq(1-p)^{k} for all k∈ℕ,0<Δ​t≤Δ​t0k\in\mathbb{N},~0<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}. For any t≥0t\geq 0 with k​T∗≤t<(k+1)​T∗kT_{\ast}\leq t<(k+1)T_{\ast}, we have {τΔ​t>t}⊂{τΔ​t>k​T∗}\{\tau_{\Delta}t>t\}\subset\{\tau_{\Delta}t>kT_{\ast}\}, so the same bound holds with tt in place of k​T∗kT_{\ast}.

Proceeding as in the proof of Theorem C.1, we use the representation 𝔼y​[eλ​τΔ​t]=1+∫0∞λ​eλ​t​ℙy​(τΔ​t>t)​𝑑t\mathbb{E}^{y}[e^{\lambda\tau_{\Delta}t}]=1+\int_{0}^{\infty}\lambda e^{\lambda t}\mathbb{P}^{y}(\tau_{\Delta}t>t)\,dt, and split the integral over the intervals [k​T∗,(k+1)​T∗)[kT_{\ast},(k+1)T_{\ast}), yielding a geometric series upper bound by the previous paragraph.

Choosing λd>0\lambda_{d}>0 so small that eλd​T∗​(1−p)<1e^{\lambda_{d}T_{\ast}}(1-p)<1, the series in question converges and its sum is finite and independent of yy and Δ​t∈(0,Δ​t0]\Delta t\in(0,\Delta t_{0}]. This gives the claimed bound with some finite constant CdC_{d}. ∎

C.3 Exponential moments and tails for the payoff

We now transfer the exponential-moment bounds for τ\tau and τΔ​t\tau_{\Delta t} to the payoffs YY and YΔ​tY^{\Delta t}.

Lemma C.5 (Deterministic bound for YΔ​tY^{\Delta t}).

Assume that ff and gg are bounded and that V≥0V\geq 0 on Ω¯\overline{\Omega}. Then there exist constants Cf,Cg≥0C_{f},C_{g}\geq 0 such that respectively for all x∈Ω¯x\in\overline{\Omega}, z∈∂Ωz\in\partial\Omega, we have |f​(x)|≤Cf\lvert f(x)\rvert\leq C_{f}, |g​(z)|≤Cg\lvert g(z)\rvert\leq C_{g}, and

|YΔ​t|≤Cf​τΔ​t+Cg​almost surely.\lvert Y^{\Delta t}\rvert\leq C_{f}\tau_{\Delta t}+C_{g}\ \text{almost surely}.
Proof.

By boundedness of ff and gg there exist Cf,Cg≥0C_{f},C_{g}\geq 0 with the stated properties. Since V≥0V\geq 0, all exponential factors in (C.5) are bounded by one. Thus

|YΔ​t|\displaystyle\lvert Y^{\Delta t}\rvert ≤∑k=0NΔ​t−1|f​(XkΔ​t)|​Δ​t+|g​(XNΔ​tΔ​t)|\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{N_{\Delta t}-1}\lvert f(X_{k}^{\Delta t})\rvert\,\Delta t+\lvert g(X_{N_{\Delta t}}^{\Delta t})\rvert
≤Cf​NΔ​t​Δ​t+Cg=Cf​τΔ​t+Cg.\displaystyle\leq C_{f}N_{\Delta t}\Delta t+C_{g}=C_{f}\tau_{\Delta t}+C_{g}.

∎

A similar argument yields a deterministic bound for YY in terms of τ\tau:

Lemma C.6 (Deterministic bound for YY).

Under the same assumptions as in Lemma C.5, one has

|Y|≤Cf​τ+Cg​almost surely.\lvert Y\rvert\leq C_{f}\tau+C_{g}\ \text{almost surely}.

Combining these bounds with Theorem C.1 and Proposition C.4, we obtain exponential moments for the payoffs.

Proposition C.7 (Exponential moments for YY and YΔ​tY^{\Delta t}).

Under the standing assumptions and assuming in addition that V≥0V\geq 0 on Ω¯\overline{\Omega}, there exist constants λY>0\lambda_{Y}>0, CY<∞C_{Y}<\infty and Δ​t0>0\Delta t_{0}>0 such that

supy∈Ω¯𝔼y​[eλY​|Y|]≤CY,\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega}}\mathbb{E}^{y}\big[e^{\lambda_{Y}\lvert Y\rvert}\big]\;\leq\;C_{Y},

and

supy∈Ω¯, 0<Δ​t≤Δ​t0𝔼y​[eλY​|YΔ​t|]≤CY.\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega},\,0<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}}\mathbb{E}^{y}\big[e^{\lambda_{Y}\lvert Y^{\Delta t}\rvert}\big]\;\leq\;C_{Y}.
Proof.

By Lemma C.5,

eλ​|YΔ​t|≤eλ​Cg​eλ​Cf​τΔ​t,e^{\lambda\lvert Y^{\Delta t}\rvert}\leq e^{\lambda C_{g}}e^{\lambda C_{f}\tau_{\Delta t}},

and by Lemma C.6,

eλ​|Y|≤eλ​Cg​eλ​Cf​τ.e^{\lambda\lvert Y\rvert}\leq e^{\lambda C_{g}}e^{\lambda C_{f}\tau}.

Using Theorem C.1 and Proposition C.4, choose λY>0\lambda_{Y}>0 small enough that λY​Cf<λc\lambda_{Y}C_{f}<\lambda_{c} and λY​Cf<λd\lambda_{Y}C_{f}<\lambda_{d}. Then the stated bounds follow immediately, with

CY:=eλY​Cg​max⁡{Cc,Cd}.C_{Y}:=e^{\lambda_{Y}C_{g}}\max\{C_{c},C_{d}\}.

∎

Remark C.8 (Sub-exponential character of YY and YΔ​tY^{\Delta t}).

A real-valued random variable ZZ is sub-exponential if there exists α>0\alpha>0 with 𝔼​[eλ​Z]<∞\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda Z}]<\infty for all |λ|<α|\lambda|<\alpha. Proposition C.7 shows that YY and YΔ​tY^{\Delta t} are sub-exponential, with sub-exponential norms bounded uniformly in Δ​t\Delta t for Δ​t≤Δ​t0\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}.

C.4 Concentration for the Monte Carlo estimator at fixed Δ​t\Delta t

We now derive non-asymptotic tail bounds for the Monte Carlo estimator u^MC​(x)\widehat{u}^{\mathrm{MC}}(x) at a fixed time step Δ​t≤Δ​t0\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}. The key tool is a Bernstein-type inequality for sub-exponential random variables.

C.4.1 A Bernstein inequality for sub-exponential variables

Theorem C.9 (Bernstein inequality for sub-exponential variables).

Let Z1,…,ZNZ_{1},\dots,Z_{N} be i.i.d. real-valued random variables with 𝔼​[Zi]=0\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}]=0 and suppose there exist constants ν2,b>0\nu^{2},b>0 satisfying

𝔼​[eλ​Zi]≤exp⁡(ν2​λ22)​ for all ​|λ|<1/b.\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\lambda Z_{i}}\big]\leq\exp\Bigl(\frac{\nu^{2}\lambda^{2}}{2}\Bigr)\ \text{ for all }\lvert\lambda\rvert<1/b.

Then there exists a universal constant c>0c>0 such that, for all t>0t>0,

ℙ​(|1N​∑i=1NZi|>t)≤2​exp⁡(−c​N​min⁡(t2ν2,tb)).\mathbb{P}\Big(\Big\lvert\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}\Big\rvert>t\Big)\leq 2\exp\Big(-cN\min\Big(\frac{t^{2}}{\nu^{2}},\frac{t}{b}\Big)\Big).
Proof.

See, for example, (Vershynin, 2018, Theorem 2.9.1). ∎

C.4.2 Application to the Euler payoff

We apply Theorem C.9 to the centered Euler payoff YΔ​t−uΔ​t​(x)Y^{\Delta t}-u_{\Delta t}(x).

Lemma C.10 (Sub-exponential parameters for YΔ​t−uΔ​t​(x)Y^{\Delta t}-u_{\Delta t}(x)).

Under the standing assumptions, there exist constants ν>0\nu>0, b>0b>0 and Δ​t0>0\Delta t_{0}>0 such that, for all Δ​t≤Δ​t0\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}, the centered random variable ZΔ​t:=YΔ​t−uΔ​t​(x)Z^{\Delta t}:=Y^{\Delta t}-u_{\Delta t}(x) satisfies

𝔼​[eλ​ZΔ​t]≤exp⁡(ν2​λ22)​for all ​|λ|<1/b.\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\lambda Z^{\Delta t}}\big]\leq\exp\Bigl(\frac{\nu^{2}\lambda^{2}}{2}\Bigr)\ \text{for all }\lvert\lambda\rvert<1/b.

The constants ν\nu and bb depend only on the model data and can be chosen independent of Δ​t≤Δ​t0\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}.

Proof.

Proposition C.7 guarantees that there exist λY>0\lambda_{Y}>0 and CY<∞C_{Y}<\infty such that

sup0<Δ​t≤Δ​t0𝔼​[eλY​|YΔ​t|]≤CY.\sup_{0<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}}\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\lambda_{Y}\lvert Y^{\Delta t}\rvert}\big]\leq C_{Y}.

This implies that the moment generating function 𝔼​[eλ​YΔ​t]\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda Y^{\Delta t}}] is finite on (−λY,λY)(-\lambda_{Y},\lambda_{Y}) uniformly in Δ​t≤Δ​t0\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}. Since ZΔ​t=YΔ​t−uΔ​t​(x)Z^{\Delta t}=Y^{\Delta t}-u_{\Delta t}(x) differs from YΔ​tY^{\Delta t} by a constant shift, the same holds for ZΔ​tZ^{\Delta t}.

A standard argument (see Vershynin (2018, Section 2.7)) shows that there exist parameters (ν,b)(\nu,b) depending only on the exponential-moment bounds of YΔ​tY^{\Delta t} such that

𝔼​[eλ​ZΔ​t]≤exp⁡(ν2​λ22)​for all ​|λ|<1/b,\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\lambda Z^{\Delta t}}\big]\leq\exp\Bigl(\frac{\nu^{2}\lambda^{2}}{2}\Bigr)\ \text{for all }\lvert\lambda\rvert<1/b,

uniformly over Δ​t≤Δ​t0\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}. We refer the reader to said reference for details. ∎

Combining Lemma C.10 with Theorem C.9 yields the following concentration inequality.

Proposition C.11 (Concentration for the Monte Carlo error at fixed Δ​t\Delta t).

Under the standing assumptions, there exist constants c>0c>0, ν>0\nu>0, b>0b>0 and Δ​t0>0\Delta t_{0}>0 such that for all Δ​t≤Δ​t0\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}, all NMC∈ℕN_{\mathrm{MC}}\in\mathbb{N} and all t>0t>0,

ℙ​(|u^MC​(x)−uΔ​t​(x)|>t)≤2​exp⁡(−c​NMC​min⁡(t2ν2,tb)).\mathbb{P}\Big(\lvert\widehat{u}^{\mathrm{MC}}(x)-u_{\Delta t}(x)\rvert>t\Big)\leq 2\exp\Big(-cN_{\mathrm{MC}}\min\Big(\frac{t^{2}}{\nu^{2}},\frac{t}{b}\Big)\Big).
Proof.

For fixed xx, Δ​t\Delta t and NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}}, define ZiΔ​t:=YΔ​t,(i)−uΔ​t​(x)Z^{\Delta t}_{i}:=Y^{\Delta t,(i)}-u_{\Delta t}(x) for i=1,…,NMCi=1,\dots,N_{\mathrm{MC}}. These variables are i.i.d. with zero mean, and by Lemma C.10 they satisfy the moment generating function condition of Theorem C.9 with parameters (ν,b)(\nu,b) independent of Δ​t≤Δ​t0\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}. Since

u^MC​(x)−uΔ​t​(x)=1NMC​∑i=1NMCZiΔ​t,\widehat{u}^{\mathrm{MC}}(x)-u_{\Delta t}(x)=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{MC}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{MC}}}Z^{\Delta t}_{i},

Theorem C.9 yields the stated inequality. ∎

Remark C.12 (sub-Gaussian vs exponential regimes).

The bound in Proposition C.11 has two regimes. For deviations 0<t≤ν2/b0<t\leq\nu^{2}/b, the quadratic term dominates and the tails behave essentially like exp⁡(−c​NMC​t2/ν2)\exp(-cN_{\mathrm{MC}}t^{2}/\nu^{2}). For larger deviations, the linear term dominates and the decay is of order exp⁡(−c​NMC​t/b)\exp(-cN_{\mathrm{MC}}t/b). In both cases the constants are independent of NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}} and of Δ​t\Delta t for Δ​t≤Δ​t0\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}.

C.5 Discretization bias

We next bound the bias uΔ​t​(x)−u⋆​(x)u_{\Delta t}(x)-u^{\star}(x) of the time-discretized FK value.

Theorem C.13 (Weak error for killed Euler schemes).

Assume that Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is a bounded C2C^{2} domain with non-characteristic boundary, that the coefficients b,σb,\sigma in (C.1) are Cb4C_{b}^{4} with bounded derivatives up to order 44, and that f,g,Vf,g,V are bounded with bounded derivatives up to the necessary order. Then there exist constants Cbias<∞C_{\mathrm{bias}}<\infty and Δ​t0>0\Delta t_{0}>0 such that, for all 0<Δ​t≤Δ​t00<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0},

|uΔ​t​(x)−u⋆​(x)|≤Cbias​Δ​t.\lvert u_{\Delta t}(x)-u^{\star}(x)\rvert\leq C_{\mathrm{bias}}\,\sqrt{\Delta t}.
Proof.

This is a specialization of the weak error estimates for killed Euler schemes in (Gobet, 2000, Theorem 2.4) and (Gobet and Menozzi, 2010, Theorem 17). Our assumptions on the regularity of b,σ,f,g,Vb,\sigma,f,g,V and on the geometry of Ω\Omega are stronger than those in the cited papers, so their hypotheses are satisfied. The functional YΔ​tY^{\Delta t} in (C.5) matches the discretization considered there. The stated bound follows, with a constant CbiasC_{\mathrm{bias}} independent of Δ​t\Delta t for Δ​t\Delta t small enough. ∎

Lemma C.14 (Bias due to time truncation).

Assume the standing assumptions of this appendix and those of Lemma C.5. Then there exist constants λ~>0\tilde{\lambda}>0, CT<∞C_{T}<\infty and Δ​t0>0\Delta t_{0}>0 such that, for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega, all 0<Δ​t≤Δ​t00<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0} and all Tmax>0T_{\max}>0,

|uΔ​tTmax​(x)−uΔ​t​(x)|≤CT​e−λ~​Tmax.\lvert u_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}(x)-u_{\Delta t}(x)\rvert\leq C_{T}e^{-\tilde{\lambda}T_{\max}}.
Proof.

On the event {τΔ​t≤Tmax}\{\tau_{\Delta t}\leq T_{\max}\} the discrete trajectory exits Ω\Omega before the truncation horizon and κΔ​tTmax=NΔ​t\kappa_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}=N_{\Delta t}, hence YΔ​t,Tmax=YΔ​tY^{\Delta t,T_{\max}}=Y^{\Delta t}. On the complement {τΔ​t>Tmax}\{\tau_{\Delta t}>T_{\max}\} the payoffs YΔ​tY^{\Delta t} and YΔ​t,TmaxY^{\Delta t,T_{\max}} differ only through the contribution of the running functional ff after time TmaxT_{\max} and through the terminal term that involves gg. Using the representation (C.5) and the definition (C.7), together with boundedness of ff and gg and the fact that all exponential factors are at most one, we obtain

|YΔ​t−YΔ​t,Tmax|≤Cf​τΔ​t​𝟏{τΔ​t>Tmax}+2​Cg​𝟏{τΔ​t>Tmax},\lvert Y^{\Delta t}-Y^{\Delta t,T_{\max}}\rvert\leq C_{f}\tau_{\Delta t}\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{\Delta t}>T_{\max}\}}+2C_{g}\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{\Delta t}>T_{\max}\}},

with the constants CfC_{f} and CgC_{g} from Lemma C.5. Taking expectations and using Proposition C.4, for any λ∈(0,λd)\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{d}),

ℙx​(τΔ​t>t)≤e−λ​t​𝔼x​[eλ​τΔ​t]≤Cd​e−λ​t,\mathbb{P}^{x}(\tau_{\Delta t}>t)\leq e^{-\lambda t}\mathbb{E}^{x}\big[e^{\lambda\tau_{\Delta t}}\big]\leq C_{d}e^{-\lambda t},

and therefore

𝔼x​[τΔ​t​𝟏{τΔ​t>Tmax}]=∫Tmax∞ℙx​(τΔ​t>u)​𝑑u≤Cdλ​e−λ​Tmax,\mathbb{E}^{x}\big[\tau_{\Delta t}\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{\Delta t}>T_{\max}\}}\big]=\int_{T_{\max}}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}^{x}(\tau_{\Delta t}>u)\,du\leq\frac{C_{d}}{\lambda}e^{-\lambda T_{\max}},

as well as

ℙx​(τΔ​t>Tmax)≤Cd​e−λ​Tmax.\mathbb{P}^{x}(\tau_{\Delta t}>T_{\max})\leq C_{d}e^{-\lambda T_{\max}}.

Combining these bounds yields

|uΔ​tTmax​(x)−uΔ​t​(x)|=|𝔼x​[YΔ​t,Tmax−YΔ​t]|≤(Cf​Cdλ+2​Cg​Cd)​e−λ​Tmax.\lvert u_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}(x)-u_{\Delta t}(x)\rvert=\lvert\mathbb{E}^{x}\big[Y^{\Delta t,T_{\max}}-Y^{\Delta t}\big]\rvert\leq\Bigl(\frac{C_{f}C_{d}}{\lambda}+2C_{g}C_{d}\Bigr)e^{-\lambda T_{\max}}.

The claim follows by setting λ~:=λ\tilde{\lambda}:=\lambda and CT:=Cf​Cdλ+2​Cg​CdC_{T}:=\frac{C_{f}C_{d}}{\lambda}+2C_{g}C_{d}, and by choosing Δ​t0\Delta t_{0} as in Proposition C.4. ∎

These bounds summarize the non-asymptotic behavior of the infinite horizon Monte Carlo FK estimator at a fixed point xx. For the learning-theoretic analysis we only need that, for each fixed xx, the FK label produced by Algorithm 1 behaves like a noisy point evaluation of u⋆​(x)u^{\star}(x) with sub-exponential noise whose parameters do not depend on the number of FK labels or on the Monte Carlo budget. This is precisely the content of Proposition 6.1 in the main text, whose proof we now provide.

Proof of Proposition 6.1.

Fix x∈Ωx\in\Omega and consider the FK estimator produced at this spatial point by Algorithm 1, with time step 0<Δ​t≤Δ​t00<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}, truncation horizon Tmax∈(0,∞]T_{\max}\in(0,\infty] and Monte Carlo budget NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}}. For each trajectory we simulate a payoff YΔ​t,TmaxY^{\Delta t,T_{\max}} as in (C.7). The FK label at xx is the empirical average of NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}} independent copies of YΔ​t,TmaxY^{\Delta t,T_{\max}}, that is

u^Tmax​(x):=1NMC​∑i=1NMCYΔ​t,Tmax,(i).\widehat{u}^{T_{\max}}(x):=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{MC}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{MC}}}Y^{\Delta t,T_{\max},(i)}.

Step 1: sub-exponential Monte Carlo fluctuations.

We distinguish the cases Tmax<∞T_{\max}<\infty and Tmax=∞T_{\max}=\infty.

If Tmax<∞T_{\max}<\infty, then at most NT=⌊Tmax/Δ​t⌋N_{T}=\lfloor T_{\max}/\Delta t\rfloor time steps are accumulated before truncation. Boundedness of ff and gg and nonnegativity of VV imply (as in Lemma C.5) the deterministic bound

|YΔ​t,Tmax|≤Cf​Tmax+Cg​ almost surely,\lvert Y^{\Delta t,T_{\max}}\rvert\leq C_{f}T_{\max}+C_{g}\ \text{ almost surely,}

uniformly in xx and 0<Δ​t≤Δ​t00<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}. Hence, for each fixed xx, the centered variable

ZΔ​t,Tmax:=YΔ​t,Tmax−uΔ​tTmax​(x)Z^{\Delta t,T_{\max}}:=Y^{\Delta t,T_{\max}}-u_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}(x)

is bounded and therefore sub-exponential, with parameters that depend only on CfC_{f}, CgC_{g} and TmaxT_{\max} and do not depend on NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}} or on the number of FK points. Standard properties of sub-exponential variables (see, e.g., Vershynin (2018, Section 2.7)) imply that empirical averages of i.i.d. sub-exponential variables are again sub-exponential, and the sub-exponential parameters can be chosen independently of the sample size. Thus, conditional on X0=xX_{0}=x,

u^Tmax​(x)−uΔ​tTmax​(x)=1NMC​∑i=1NMCZΔ​t,Tmax,(i)\widehat{u}^{T_{\max}}(x)-u_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}(x)=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{MC}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{MC}}}Z^{\Delta t,T_{\max},(i)}

is mean-zero and sub-exponential with parameters depending only on the problem data and on TmaxT_{\max}, and not on NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}}.

If Tmax=∞T_{\max}=\infty, then YΔ​t,∞=YΔ​tY^{\Delta t,\infty}=Y^{\Delta t} and uΔ​t∞​(x)=uΔ​t​(x)u_{\Delta t}^{\infty}(x)=u_{\Delta t}(x). Proposition C.7 yields constants λY>0\lambda_{Y}>0, CY<∞C_{Y}<\infty and Δ​t0>0\Delta t_{0}>0 such that

supy∈Ω¯, 0<Δ​t≤Δ​t0𝔼y​[eλY​|YΔ​t|]≤CY.\sup_{y\in\overline{\Omega},\,0<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}}\mathbb{E}^{y}\big[e^{\lambda_{Y}\lvert Y^{\Delta t}\rvert}\big]\;\leq\;C_{Y}.

In particular, for each fixed xx and 0<Δ​t≤Δ​t00<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}, the centered variable

ZΔ​t:=YΔ​t−uΔ​t​(x)Z^{\Delta t}:=Y^{\Delta t}-u_{\Delta t}(x)

is sub-exponential with parameters depending only on CYC_{Y} and λY\lambda_{Y} and independent of Δ​t\Delta t, NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}} and the number of FK points, as per Lemma C.10. As in the finite-horizon case, empirical averages of i.i.d. copies of ZΔ​tZ^{\Delta t} are again sub-exponential, with parameters that can be chosen independent of NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}}. Thus u^∞​(x)−uΔ​t​(x)\widehat{u}^{\infty}(x)-u_{\Delta t}(x) is mean-zero and sub-exponential with parameters depending only on the model data.

In both cases we may therefore write

u^Tmax​(x)=uΔ​tTmax​(x)+ζ​(x),\widehat{u}^{T_{\max}}(x)=u_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}(x)+\zeta(x),

where, conditional on X0=xX_{0}=x, the fluctuation ζ​(x)\zeta(x) is mean-zero and sub-exponential with parameters that do not depend on NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}} or on the number of FK points (and are uniform over 0<Δ​t≤Δ​t00<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}).

Step 2: discretization and truncation bias.

We now decompose the bias of the (possibly truncated) FK value. Adding and subtracting uΔ​t​(x)u_{\Delta t}(x) and u⋆​(x)u^{\star}(x) yields

u^Tmax​(x)=u⋆​(x)+(uΔ​t​(x)−u⋆​(x))+(uΔ​tTmax​(x)−uΔ​t​(x))+ζ​(x).\widehat{u}^{T_{\max}}(x)=u^{\star}(x)+\bigl(u_{\Delta t}(x)-u^{\star}(x)\bigr)+\bigl(u_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}(x)-u_{\Delta t}(x)\bigr)+\zeta(x).

By Theorem C.13 the discretization bias satisfies

|uΔ​t​(x)−u⋆​(x)|≤Cbias​Δ​t, for all ​0<Δ​t≤Δ​t0,\lvert u_{\Delta t}(x)-u^{\star}(x)\rvert\leq C_{\mathrm{bias}}\sqrt{\Delta t},\ \text{ for all }0<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0},

while Lemma C.14 gives

|uΔ​tTmax​(x)−uΔ​t​(x)|≤CT​e−λ~​Tmax,for all ​Tmax>0,\lvert u_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}(x)-u_{\Delta t}(x)\rvert\leq C_{T}e^{-\tilde{\lambda}T_{\max}},\ \text{for all }T_{\max}>0,

with the convention e−λ~​Tmax=0e^{-\tilde{\lambda}T_{\max}}=0 when Tmax=∞T_{\max}=\infty. Defining

b​(x):=(uΔ​t​(x)−u⋆​(x))+(uΔ​tTmax​(x)−uΔ​t​(x)),b(x):=\bigl(u_{\Delta t}(x)-u^{\star}(x)\bigr)+\bigl(u_{\Delta t}^{T_{\max}}(x)-u_{\Delta t}(x)\bigr),

we obtain the decomposition

u^Tmax​(x)=u⋆​(x)+b​(x)+ζ​(x),\widehat{u}^{T_{\max}}(x)=u^{\star}(x)+b(x)+\zeta(x),

with

|b​(x)|≤Cbias​Δ​t+CT​e−λ~​Tmax,\lvert b(x)\rvert\leq C_{\mathrm{bias}}\sqrt{\Delta t}+C_{T}e^{-\tilde{\lambda}T_{\max}},

and with ζ​(x)\zeta(x) mean-zero and sub-exponential with parameters independent of NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}} and of the number of FK points, uniformly over 0<Δ​t≤Δ​t00<\Delta t\leq\Delta t_{0}.

Step 3: random FK locations. In the FK-PINN construction we draw i.i.d. supervision locations XiFK∈ΩX_{i}^{\mathrm{FK}}\in\Omega, and at each such point we compute an independent estimator u^Tmax​(XiFK)\widehat{u}^{T_{\max}}(X_{i}^{\mathrm{FK}}) using a fresh set of NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}} trajectories. Setting

YiFK:=u^Tmax​(XiFK),b​(XiFK):=b​(XiFK),ζi:=ζ​(XiFK),Y_{i}^{\mathrm{FK}}:=\widehat{u}^{T_{\max}}(X_{i}^{\mathrm{FK}}),\quad b(X_{i}^{\mathrm{FK}}):=b\bigl(X_{i}^{\mathrm{FK}}\bigr),\quad\zeta_{i}:=\zeta\bigl(X_{i}^{\mathrm{FK}}\bigr),

the pairs {(XiFK,YiFK)}i=1NFK\{(X_{i}^{\mathrm{FK}},Y_{i}^{\mathrm{FK}})\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{FK}}} are i.i.d., and, conditional on XiFK=xX_{i}^{\mathrm{FK}}=x, each YiFKY_{i}^{\mathrm{FK}} admits the decomposition

YiFK=u⋆​(x)+b​(x)+ζi,Y_{i}^{\mathrm{FK}}=u^{\star}(x)+b(x)+\zeta_{i},

with |b​(x)|≤Cbias​Δ​t+CT​e−λ~​Tmax\lvert b(x)\rvert\leq C_{\mathrm{bias}}\sqrt{\Delta t}+C_{T}e^{-\tilde{\lambda}T_{\max}} and with ζi\zeta_{i} mean-zero and sub-exponential with parameters that do not depend on NFKN_{\mathrm{FK}} or NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}}. This is exactly the statement in Proposition 6.1, thus we are done.

Appendix D Error Analysis for FK-PINNs

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem 6.2. To this end, we will develop a comprehensive error analysis, based on a decomposition of the L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) error in three terms, which we will control separately through learning-theoretic arguments.

D.1 Preliminaries

We begin by recalling the setting in which we will be working together with notations and technical assumptions that we will be working under for the remainder of this section.

D.1.1 Notations

We work on a bounded Lipschitz domain Ω⊂[0,1]d\Omega\subset[0,1]^{d} with boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega and outward unit normal ν\nu. Integration with respect to Lebesgue measure on Ω\Omega is written as ∫Ω⋅d​x\int_{\Omega}\cdot\,dx, while ∫∂Ω⋅d​s\int_{\partial\Omega}\cdot\,ds denotes integration with respect to surface measure on ∂Ω\partial\Omega.

For 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty we write Lp​(Ω)L^{p}(\Omega) and Lp​(∂Ω)L^{p}(\partial\Omega) for the usual Lebesgue spaces, with norms

∥u∥Lp​(Ω):={(∫Ω|u​(x)|p​𝑑x)1/p,1≤p<∞,ess​supx∈Ω⁡|u​(x)|,p=∞,\lVert u\rVert_{L^{p}(\Omega)}:=\begin{cases}\bigl(\int_{\Omega}|u(x)|^{p}\,dx\bigr)^{1/p},&1\leq p<\infty,\\[1.99997pt] \operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in\Omega}|u(x)|,&p=\infty,\end{cases}

and similarly on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. We write C​(Ω¯)C(\overline{\Omega}) for the space of continuous functions on the closure of Ω\Omega with norm ∥u∥C​(Ω¯):=supx∈Ω¯|u​(x)|\lVert u\rVert_{C(\overline{\Omega})}:=\sup_{x\in\overline{\Omega}}|u(x)|.

For s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N} and 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty, the Sobolev space Ws,p​(Ω)W^{s,p}(\Omega) consists of functions in Lp​(Ω)L^{p}(\Omega) whose weak derivatives up to order ss lie in Lp​(Ω)L^{p}(\Omega), endowed with norm

∥u∥Ws,p​(Ω):=(∑|α|≤s∥Dα​u∥Lp​(Ω)p)1/pfor ​p<∞,\lVert u\rVert_{W^{s,p}(\Omega)}:=\biggl(\sum_{|\alpha|\leq s}\lVert D^{\alpha}u\rVert_{L^{p}(\Omega)}^{p}\biggr)^{1/p}\quad\text{for }p<\infty,

and with the obvious modification for p=∞p=\infty. We use Hs​(Ω):=Ws,2​(Ω)H^{s}(\Omega):=W^{s,2}(\Omega). Fractional Sobolev spaces Hs​(Ω)H^{s}(\Omega) for s∉ℕs\notin\mathbb{N} are defined in the standard way, for instance via real interpolation or via the Gagliardo seminorm, see Evans (2022). We denote the associated norms by ∥⋅∥Hs​(Ω)\lVert\cdot\rVert_{H^{s}(\Omega)}.

Throughout, ⟨⋅⟩⋅\langle\cdot\rangle{\cdot} denotes the L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) inner product, and ∥⋅∥L2​(Ω)\lVert\cdot\rVert_{L^{2}(\Omega)} is abbreviated to ∥⋅∥2\lVert\cdot\rVert_{2} when the domain is clear from the context. For random variables we write 𝔼​[⋅]\mathbb{E}[\cdot] for expectation and ℙ​(⋅)\mathbb{P}(\cdot) for probabilities.

D.1.2 Setting and Assumptions

We recall the PDE from Section 2.1. Throughout this appendix we work in the elliptic setting for clarity. All statements are formulated and proved for the second order elliptic problem in (2.1)–(2.2). The same learning theoretic arguments extend to parabolic problems that admit a Feynman–Kac representation, once the time variable has been discretized and the resulting time discretization error is controlled separately. Since this would require additional notation and is orthogonal to the main message of the paper, we do not pursue the parabolic case in detail here.

Assumption D.1 (PDE well posedness and FK representation).

The operator ℒ\mathcal{L} in (2.1) is uniformly elliptic with bounded measurable coefficients and satisfies the structural conditions stated in Section 2.1. The data ff and gg are such that (2.1)–(2.2) admit a unique strong solution

u⋆∈H2​(Ω)∩C​(Ω¯),u^{\star}\in H^{2}(\Omega)\cap C(\overline{\Omega}),

with u⋆|∂Ω=gu^{\star}|_{\partial\Omega}=g. Moreover, there exists a diffusion process (Xt)t≥0(X_{t})_{t\geq 0} and an exit time τ\tau such that u⋆u^{\star} admits a Feynman–Kac representation of the form

u⋆​(x)=𝔼x​[∫0τr​(Xt)​𝑑t+h​(Xτ)],x∈Ω,u^{\star}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{x}\Bigl[\int_{0}^{\tau}r(X_{t})\,dt+h(X_{\tau})\Bigr],\quad x\in\Omega,

for suitable running and terminal functionals rr and hh, as described in Section 3 and Appendix A.

We follow the sampling scheme described in Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2. Let

Xint∼U​(Ω),X∂Ω∼U​(∂Ω),X^{\mathrm{int}}\sim U(\Omega),\qquad X^{\partial\Omega}\sim U(\partial\Omega),

be interior and boundary points drawn independently from the uniform distributions on Ω\Omega and ∂Ω\partial\Omega. The corresponding population PDE and boundary risks are

ℛPDE​(u)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{PDE}}(u) :=|Ω|​𝔼​[|ℒ​u​(Xint)−f​(Xint)|2],\displaystyle:=\lvert\Omega\rvert\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\bigl|\mathcal{L}u(X^{\mathrm{int}})-f(X^{\mathrm{int}})\bigr|^{2}\bigr], (D.1)
ℛ∂Ω​(u)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\partial\Omega}(u) :=|∂Ω|​𝔼​[|u​(X∂Ω)−g​(X∂Ω)|2].\displaystyle:=\lvert\partial\Omega\rvert\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\bigl|u(X^{\partial\Omega})-g(X^{\partial\Omega})\bigr|^{2}\bigr]. (D.2)

In the FK term we work in a data scarce regime. We sample FK points from the same underlying geometry as the interior points, but we keep their number small. Concretely, we assume

XFK∼U​(Ω),X^{\mathrm{FK}}\sim U(\Omega),

independently of XintX^{\mathrm{int}} and X∂ΩX^{\partial\Omega}, while the sample size NFKN_{\mathrm{FK}} is allowed to remain bounded or grow much more slowly than NintN_{\mathrm{int}} and N∂ΩN_{\partial\Omega}. At each such point we generate a Monte Carlo FK estimate u^MC​(XFK)\widehat{u}^{\mathrm{MC}}(X^{\mathrm{FK}}) as in Algorithm 1. Proposition 6.1 shows that these labels admit the decomposition

u^MC​(XFK)=u⋆​(XFK)+b​(XFK)+ζ,\widehat{u}^{\mathrm{MC}}(X^{\mathrm{FK}})=u^{\star}(X^{\mathrm{FK}})+b(X^{\mathrm{FK}})+\zeta,

where the deterministic bias b:Ω→ℝb:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} satisfies

|b​(x)|≤Cbias​Δ​t+CT​e−κ​Tmaxfor all ​x∈Ω,\lvert b(x)\rvert\leq C_{\mathrm{bias}}\sqrt{\Delta t}+C_{T}e^{-\kappa T_{\max}}\quad\text{for all }x\in\Omega,

for constants Cbias,CT,κ>0C_{\mathrm{bias}},C_{T},\kappa>0 independent of NFKN_{\mathrm{FK}} and of the number of FK trajectories, and where, conditional on XFKX^{\mathrm{FK}}, the fluctuation ζ\zeta is mean-zero and sub-exponential with parameters that do not depend on NFKN_{\mathrm{FK}} or on the number of trajectories. The corresponding population FK risk is

ℛFK​(u):=𝔼​[|u​(XFK)−u⋆​(XFK)|2].\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{FK}}(u):=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\bigl|u(X^{\mathrm{FK}})-u^{\star}(X^{\mathrm{FK}})\bigr|^{2}\bigr]. (D.3)

For fixed nonnegative weights λPDE\lambda_{\mathrm{PDE}}, λ∂Ω\lambda_{\partial\Omega} and λFK\lambda_{\mathrm{FK}} we define the population FK-PINN risk

ℛ​(u):=λPDE​ℛPDE​(u)+λ∂Ω​ℛ∂Ω​(u)+λFK​ℛFK​(u).\mathcal{R}(u):=\lambda_{\mathrm{PDE}}\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{PDE}}(u)+\lambda_{\partial\Omega}\mathcal{R}_{\partial\Omega}(u)+\lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{FK}}(u). (D.4)

In what follows we assume that the PDE and boundary weights λPDE,λ∂Ω\lambda_{\mathrm{PDE}},\lambda_{\partial\Omega}, and that the FK weight is non-negative. For convenience, we will use the abbreviation

λmin:=min⁡{λPDE,λ∂Ω}.\lambda_{\min}:=\min\{\lambda_{\mathrm{PDE}},\lambda_{\partial\Omega}\}.

Note that rescaling the three weights only changes the constants in the bounds below, so this choice entails no loss of generality. The empirical FK-PINN risk is obtained by Monte Carlo approximation of the expectations in (D.1)–(D.3). Given i.i.d. samples

{xiint}i=1Nint⊂Ω,{xj∂Ω}j=1N∂Ω⊂∂Ω,{xkFK}k=1NFK⊂Ω,\{x_{i}^{\mathrm{int}}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{int}}}\subset\Omega,\quad\{x_{j}^{\partial\Omega}\}_{j=1}^{N_{\partial\Omega}}\subset\partial\Omega,\quad\{x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}}\}_{k=1}^{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}\subset\Omega,

and the corresponding FK labels {u^MC​(xkFK)}k=1NFK\{\widehat{u}^{\mathrm{MC}}(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}})\}_{k=1}^{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}, we set

ℛ^PDE​(u)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{PDE}}(u) :=|Ω|​1Nint​∑i=1Nint|ℒ​u​(xiint)−f​(xiint)|2,\displaystyle:=\lvert\Omega\rvert\,\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{int}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{int}}}\bigl|\mathcal{L}u(x_{i}^{\mathrm{int}})-f(x_{i}^{\mathrm{int}})\bigr|^{2}, (D.5)
ℛ^∂Ω​(u)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\partial\Omega}(u) :=|∂Ω|​1N∂Ω​∑j=1N∂Ω|u​(xj∂Ω)−g​(xj∂Ω)|2,\displaystyle:=\lvert\partial\Omega\rvert\,\frac{1}{N_{\partial\Omega}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\partial\Omega}}\bigl|u(x_{j}^{\partial\Omega})-g(x_{j}^{\partial\Omega})\bigr|^{2}, (D.6)
ℛ^FK​(u)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{FK}}(u) :=1NFK​∑k=1NFK|u​(xkFK)−u^MC​(xkFK)|2,\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}\bigl|u(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}})-\widehat{u}^{\mathrm{MC}}(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}})\bigr|^{2}, (D.7)

and

ℛ^​(u):=λPDE​ℛ^PDE​(u)+λ∂Ω​ℛ^∂Ω​(u)+λFK​ℛ^FK​(u).\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u):=\lambda_{\mathrm{PDE}}\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{PDE}}(u)+\lambda_{\partial\Omega}\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\partial\Omega}(u)+\lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{FK}}(u). (D.8)

Up to the adaptive task weights used in Equation 4.3, the empirical loss ℛ^​(uθ)\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u_{\theta}) coincides with ℛFK​-​PINN​(θ,φ)\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{FK\text{-}PINN}}(\theta,\varphi).

We will make use of the following classical PDE estimate.

Lemma D.1 (PDE stability).

Under Assumption D.1 there exists a constant Cstab>0C_{\mathrm{stab}}>0 such that for every u∈H2​(Ω)∩C​(Ω¯)u\in H^{2}(\Omega)\cap C(\overline{\Omega}) with u|∂Ω∈L2​(∂Ω)u|_{\partial\Omega}\in L^{2}(\partial\Omega),

∥u−u⋆∥L2​(Ω)2≤Cstab​(ℛPDE​(u)+ℛ∂Ω​(u)).\lVert u-u^{\star}\rVert_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}\leq C_{\mathrm{stab}}\Bigl(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{PDE}}(u)+\mathcal{R}_{\partial\Omega}(u)\Bigr). (D.9)

Lemma D.1 is a direct consequence of the a priori boundary estimates of Agmon et al. (1959), combined with the embedding L2​(Ω)↪H−s​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow H^{-s}(\Omega) for suitable s>0s>0. One may also refer to Evans (2022, Chapter 6) and Jiao et al. (2022); Lei et al. (2025) for formulations tailored to PINNs.

We will work with a hypothesis class 𝒰\mathcal{U} of candidate solutions, specified in the next subsection. For any u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} we define

ℰapp:=infv∈𝒰∥v−u⋆∥L2​(Ω),ℰstat:=supv∈𝒰|ℛ(v)−ℛ^(v)|.\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{app}}:=\inf_{v\in\mathcal{U}}\lVert v-u^{\star}\rVert_{L^{2}(\Omega)},\qquad\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}:=\sup_{v\in\mathcal{U}}\bigl|\mathcal{R}(v)-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(v)\bigr|. (D.10)

The following decomposition is standard.

Lemma D.2 (Risk decomposition).

Let u^∈arg​minu∈𝒰⁡ℛ^​(u)\widehat{u}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u) be any empirical minimizer. Then

ℛ​(u^)−ℛ​(u⋆)≤2​ℰstat+infu∈𝒰[ℛ​(u)−ℛ​(u⋆)].\mathcal{R}(\widehat{u})-\mathcal{R}(u^{\star})\leq 2\,\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}+\inf_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\bigl[\mathcal{R}(u)-\mathcal{R}(u^{\star})\bigr]. (D.11)
Proof.

Fix any u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U}. Then

ℛ​(u^)−ℛ​(u⋆)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\widehat{u})-\mathcal{R}(u^{\star}) =(ℛ​(u^)−ℛ^​(u^))+(ℛ^​(u^)−ℛ^​(u))\displaystyle=\bigl(\mathcal{R}(\widehat{u})-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(\widehat{u})\bigr)+\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(\widehat{u})-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u)\bigr)
+(ℛ^​(u)−ℛ​(u))+(ℛ​(u)−ℛ​(u⋆)).\displaystyle\quad+\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u)-\mathcal{R}(u)\bigr)+\bigl(\mathcal{R}(u)-\mathcal{R}(u^{\star})\bigr).

By optimality of u^\widehat{u} for ℛ^\widehat{\mathcal{R}} we have ℛ^​(u^)≤ℛ^​(u)\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(\widehat{u})\leq\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u), so the middle term is nonpositive. Hence

ℛ​(u^)−ℛ​(u⋆)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\widehat{u})-\mathcal{R}(u^{\star}) ≤|ℛ​(u^)−ℛ^​(u^)|+|ℛ^​(u)−ℛ​(u)|+(ℛ​(u)−ℛ​(u⋆))\displaystyle\leq\bigl|\mathcal{R}(\widehat{u})-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(\widehat{u})\bigr|+\bigl|\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u)-\mathcal{R}(u)\bigr|+\bigl(\mathcal{R}(u)-\mathcal{R}(u^{\star})\bigr)
≤2​ℰstat+(ℛ​(u)−ℛ​(u⋆)),\displaystyle\leq 2\,\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}+\bigl(\mathcal{R}(u)-\mathcal{R}(u^{\star})\bigr),

where we used the definition of ℰstat\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}} in (D.10). Since this bound holds for every u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U}, taking the infimum over uu yields

ℛ​(u^)−ℛ​(u⋆)≤2​ℰstat+infu∈𝒰[ℛ​(u)−ℛ​(u⋆)].∎\mathcal{R}(\widehat{u})-\mathcal{R}(u^{\star})\leq 2\,\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}+\inf_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\bigl[\mathcal{R}(u)-\mathcal{R}(u^{\star})\bigr].\qed

Later we also introduce an optimization error ℰopt\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{opt}} that measures the gap between the empirical minimizer and the iterate produced by gradient descent. These three terms will form the building blocks of the final non-asymptotic bound.

D.1.3 Neural Network Architecture

We consider fully connected feedforward neural networks with tanh\tanh activations in the hidden layers and a linear output. For an integer depth L≥1L\geq 1 and a fixed width vector (mℓ)ℓ=0L(m_{\ell})_{\ell=0}^{L} with m0=dm_{0}=d and mL=1m_{L}=1, a parameter vector

𝜽:={Wℓ,bℓ}ℓ=1L,Wℓ∈ℝmℓ×mℓ−1,bℓ∈ℝmℓ,\bm{\theta}:=\bigl\{W_{\ell},b_{\ell}\bigr\}_{\ell=1}^{L},\quad W_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times m_{\ell-1}},\ b_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}},

defines a function u𝜽:Ω→ℝu_{\bm{\theta}}:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} by

z0​(x)\displaystyle z_{0}(x) :=x∈ℝd,\displaystyle:=x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, (D.12)
zℓ​(x)\displaystyle z_{\ell}(x) :=tanh⁡(Wℓ​zℓ−1​(x)+bℓ),ℓ=1,…,L−1,\displaystyle:=\tanh\bigl(W_{\ell}z_{\ell-1}(x)+b_{\ell}\bigr),\quad\ell=1,\dots,L-1, (D.13)
u𝜽​(x)\displaystyle u_{\bm{\theta}}(x) :=WL​zL−1​(x)+bL∈ℝ.\displaystyle:=W_{L}z_{L-1}(x)+b_{L}\in\mathbb{R}. (D.14)

We write P:=P​(L,(mℓ)ℓ)P:=P(L,(m_{\ell})_{\ell}) for the total number of free parameters in 𝜽\bm{\theta} and call LL the depth and m:=maxℓ⁡mℓm:=\max_{\ell}m_{\ell} the width of the network.

We will later use the following upper bound on the number of free parameters: by definition,

P=∑ℓ=1L(mℓ​mℓ−1+mℓ),m0=d,mL=1​ and ​mℓ≤m​ for all ​0≤ℓ≤L.P=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\bigl(m_{\ell}m_{\ell-1}+m_{\ell}\bigr),\ \ m_{0}=d,\ \ m_{L}=1\ \text{ and }\ m_{\ell}\leq m\text{ for all }0\leq\ell\leq L.

This implies that P≤Carch​(d)​L​m2P\leq C_{\mathrm{arch}}(d)\,L\,m^{2} for a constant Carch​(d)>0C_{\mathrm{arch}}(d)>0 depending only on the input dimension dd. In all subsequent bounds we may therefore replace PP by Carch​(d)​L​m2C_{\mathrm{arch}}(d)\,L\,m^{2} if we wish to make the dependence on the architectural hyperparameters explicit.

For the learning-theoretic analysis we restrict attention to networks whose outputs and low order derivatives are uniformly bounded on Ω¯\overline{\Omega}. For fixed LL, (mℓ)ℓ(m_{\ell})_{\ell} and B>0B>0 we first define the parameter set

ΘL,m:={𝜽=(Wℓ,bℓ)ℓ=1L:Wℓ∈ℝmℓ×mℓ−1,bℓ∈ℝmℓ}.\Theta_{L,m}:=\Bigl\{\bm{\theta}=(W_{\ell},b_{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L}:W_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times m_{\ell-1}},\ b_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}}\Bigr\}.

The associated hypothesis class is

𝒰L,m,B:={u𝜽:𝜽∈ΘL,m,∥u𝜽∥C2​(Ω¯)≤B},\mathcal{U}_{L,m,B}:=\bigl\{u_{\bm{\theta}}:\bm{\theta}\in\Theta_{L,m},\ \lVert u_{\bm{\theta}}\rVert_{C^{2}(\overline{\Omega})}\leq B\bigr\}, (D.15)

where ∥⋅∥C2​(Ω¯)\lVert\cdot\rVert_{C^{2}(\overline{\Omega})} denotes the usual C2C^{2} norm that controls the function and its first and second order partial derivatives on Ω¯\overline{\Omega}. The class 𝒰L,m,B\mathcal{U}_{L,m,B} is nonempty for every BB large enough, since constant functions belong to it.

To lighten notation we often write 𝒰\mathcal{U} for 𝒰L,m,B\mathcal{U}_{L,m,B} and denote by PP the maximal number of parameters of networks in 𝒰\mathcal{U}. All constants in the sequel may depend on (L,m,B,d)(L,m,B,d) but never on the sample sizes (Nint,N∂Ω,NFK)(N_{\mathrm{int}},N_{\partial\Omega},N_{\mathrm{FK}}).

D.2 Approximation Error Bound

We first bound the approximation error in (D.10) in terms of the size of the network. The desired bounds will directly follow from the approximation error bounds of tanh\mathrm{tanh} networks due to De Ryck et al. (2021).

Theorem D.3 (Approximation by two hidden layer tanh\tanh networks, simplified).

Let d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, let s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N} with s≥3s\geq 3 and let f∈Ws,∞​([0,1]d)f\in W^{s,\infty}([0,1]^{d}). There exist constants Capprox,Cwidth>0C_{\mathrm{approx}},C_{\mathrm{width}}>0, depending only on (d,s,∥f∥Ws,∞)(d,s,\lVert f\rVert_{W^{s,\infty}}), such that for every integer NN large enough there is a tanh\tanh network f^N\widehat{f}_{N} with two hidden layers whose total number of parameters satisfies

PN≤Cwidth​NdP_{N}\leq C_{\mathrm{width}}N^{d}

and such that, for all multi indices α\alpha with |α|≤2|\alpha|\leq 2,

∥Dα​f−Dα​f^N∥L∞​([0,1]d)≤Capprox​N−(s−|α|).\lVert D^{\alpha}f-D^{\alpha}\widehat{f}_{N}\rVert_{L^{\infty}([0,1]^{d})}\leq C_{\mathrm{approx}}N^{-(s-|\alpha|)}. (D.16)
Remark D.4.

Theorem D.3 is a mild simplification of De Ryck et al. (2021, Theorem 5.1). The original statement specifies exact widths for the two hidden layers and tracks additional logarithmic factors in NN, while we only retain the dominant polynomial dependence on NN, which is all that enters our rate calculations.

We now apply this result to the hypothesis class 𝒰\mathcal{U} defined in (D.15) and to the true solution u⋆u^{\star}.

Corollary D.5 (Approximation error for 𝒰L,m,B\mathcal{U}_{L,m,B}).

Suppose that Assumption D.1 holds and that u⋆∈Ws,∞​(Ω)u^{\star}\in W^{s,\infty}(\Omega) for some integer s≥3s\geq 3. Fix any depth L≥3L\geq 3. Then there exist constants Capp,1,Capp,2>0C_{\mathrm{app},1},C_{\mathrm{app},2}>0 and m0∈ℕm_{0}\in\mathbb{N} such that for every width m≥m0m\geq m_{0} the hypothesis class 𝒰L,m,B\mathcal{U}_{L,m,B} contains a network uapproxu^{\mathrm{approx}} with

∥u⋆−uapprox∥C2​(Ω¯)≤Capp,1​P​(L,m)−γ,γ:=s−2d,\lVert u^{\star}-u^{\mathrm{approx}}\rVert_{C^{2}(\overline{\Omega})}\leq C_{\mathrm{app},1}\,P(L,m)^{-\gamma},\qquad\gamma:=\frac{s-2}{d}, (D.17)

where P​(L,m)P(L,m) denotes the total number of free parameters of networks in 𝒰L,m,B\mathcal{U}_{L,m,B}. In particular,

ℰapp=infu∈𝒰L,m,B∥u−u⋆∥L2​(Ω)≤Capp,2​P​(L,m)−γ.\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{app}}=\inf_{u\in\mathcal{U}_{L,m,B}}\lVert u-u^{\star}\rVert_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\leq C_{\mathrm{app},2}\,P(L,m)^{-\gamma}. (D.18)
Proof.

By the Sobolev extension theorem whose conditions are satisfied here (Evans, 2022), we can extend u⋆u^{\star} to a function in Ws,∞​([0,1]d)W^{s,\infty}([0,1]^{d}) with comparable norm. Now we apply Theorem D.3 with this extension :for each integer NN large enough, we obtain a two-hidden-layer tanh\tanh network u^N\widehat{u}_{N} with depth L=3L=3, widths of order NdN^{d} in each hidden layer, total number of parameters PN≤Cwidth​NdP_{N}\leq C_{\mathrm{width}}N^{d}, and

∥Dα​u⋆−Dα​u^N∥L∞​([0,1]d)≤Capprox​N−(s−|α|),|α|≤2.\lVert D^{\alpha}u^{\star}-D^{\alpha}\widehat{u}_{N}\rVert_{L^{\infty}([0,1]^{d})}\leq C_{\mathrm{approx}}N^{-(s-|\alpha|)},\qquad|\alpha|\leq 2.

In particular,

∥u⋆−u^N∥C2​(Ω¯)≤C​N−(s−2)\lVert u^{\star}-\widehat{u}_{N}\rVert_{C^{2}(\overline{\Omega})}\leq CN^{-(s-2)}

for a constant CC depending on (d,s,∥u⋆∥Ws,∞)(d,s,\lVert u^{\star}\rVert_{W^{s,\infty}}).

Any such two-hidden-layer network can be realized as a special case of our architecture with depth L≥3L\geq 3 and width mm as soon as mm is larger than the maximal width of u^N\widehat{u}_{N}, since the extra layers and neurons can be made inactive by setting their weights to zero or to identities. Thus, for every L≥3L\geq 3 there exists m0m_{0} such that for all m≥m0m\geq m_{0} the network u^N\widehat{u}_{N} belongs to 𝒰L,m,B\mathcal{U}_{L,m,B} provided BB is chosen large enough.

Let NminN_{\min} be the (fixed) threshold required in Theorem D.3 and choose

N:=max⁡{Nmin,⌊(P​(L,m)/Cwidth)1/d⌋}.N:=\max\Bigl\{N_{\min},\,\bigl\lfloor(P(L,m)/C_{\mathrm{width}})^{1/d}\bigr\rfloor\Bigr\}.

Then PN≤Cwidth​Nd≤P​(L,m)P_{N}\leq C_{\mathrm{width}}N^{d}\leq P(L,m) and therefore

∥u⋆−u^N∥C2​(Ω¯)≤C​N−(s−2)≤C′​P​(L,m)−γ,γ=s−2d,\lVert u^{\star}-\widehat{u}_{N}\rVert_{C^{2}(\overline{\Omega})}\leq CN^{-(s-2)}\leq C^{\prime}P(L,m)^{-\gamma},\qquad\gamma=\frac{s-2}{d},

for a constant C′>0C^{\prime}>0. Taking uapprox=u^Nu^{\mathrm{approx}}=\widehat{u}_{N} yields (D.17) with Capp,1=C​C′C_{\mathrm{app},1}=CC^{\prime}. Since Ω\Omega is bounded, ∥v∥L2​(Ω)≤CΩ​∥v∥C​(Ω¯)\lVert v\rVert_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\leq C_{\Omega}\lVert v\rVert_{C(\overline{\Omega})} for every continuous vv, and (D.18) follows from (D.17) by absorbing CΩC_{\Omega} into Capp,2C_{\mathrm{app},2}. ∎

Corollary D.5 shows that ℰapp\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{app}} decays at least polynomially in the number of parameters whenever u⋆u^{\star} has Sobolev regularity of order exceeding two. Stronger, essentially exponential, rates can be obtained under analyticity assumptions on u⋆u^{\star} using De Ryck et al. (2021, Corollary 5.5), but we do not pursue this here.

Lemma D.6 (Control of the population risk by C2C^{2} approximation).

Under Assumption D.1 and with the weights (λPDE,λ∂Ω,λFK)(\lambda_{\mathrm{PDE}},\lambda_{\partial\Omega},\lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}) as in (D.4), there exists a constant Crisk>0C_{\mathrm{risk}}>0, depending only on the PDE coefficients, the domain, and the weights, such that for every u∈C2​(Ω¯)u\in C^{2}(\overline{\Omega}) with

∥u−u⋆∥C2​(Ω¯)≤ε,\lVert u-u^{\star}\rVert_{C^{2}(\overline{\Omega})}\leq\varepsilon,

one has

ℛ​(u)≤Crisk​ε2.\mathcal{R}(u)\leq C_{\mathrm{risk}}\,\varepsilon^{2}. (D.19)

In particular, for the approximating network uapproxu^{\mathrm{approx}} from Corollary D.5 we have

ℛ​(uapprox)≤C~risk​P−2​γ,\mathcal{R}(u^{\mathrm{approx}})\leq\widetilde{C}_{\mathrm{risk}}\,P^{-2\gamma}, (D.20)

for a constant C~risk>0\widetilde{C}_{\mathrm{risk}}>0 independent of PP.

Proof.

Since ℒ\mathcal{L} is a second order operator with bounded measurable coefficients, there exists a constant Cℒ>0C_{\mathcal{L}}>0 such that

supx∈Ω¯|ℒ​(u−u⋆)​(x)|≤Cℒ​∥u−u⋆∥C2​(Ω¯).\sup_{x\in\overline{\Omega}}\bigl|\mathcal{L}(u-u^{\star})(x)\bigr|\leq C_{\mathcal{L}}\,\lVert u-u^{\star}\rVert_{C^{2}(\overline{\Omega})}.

Therefore

ℛPDE​(u)=∫Ω(ℒ​u​(x)−f​(x))2​𝑑x=∫Ω(ℒ​(u−u⋆)​(x))2​𝑑x≤|Ω|​Cℒ2​ε2.\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{PDE}}(u)=\int_{\Omega}\bigl(\mathcal{L}u(x)-f(x)\bigr)^{2}\,dx=\int_{\Omega}\bigl(\mathcal{L}(u-u^{\star})(x)\bigr)^{2}\,dx\leq\lvert\Omega\rvert\,C_{\mathcal{L}}^{2}\,\varepsilon^{2}.

On the boundary we have

supx∈∂Ω|u​(x)−g​(x)|=supx∈∂Ω|u​(x)−u⋆​(x)|≤∥u−u⋆∥C​(Ω¯)≤ε,\sup_{x\in\partial\Omega}\bigl|u(x)-g(x)\bigr|=\sup_{x\in\partial\Omega}\bigl|u(x)-u^{\star}(x)\bigr|\leq\lVert u-u^{\star}\rVert_{C(\overline{\Omega})}\leq\varepsilon,

which gives

ℛ∂Ω​(u)=∫∂Ω(u​(x)−g​(x))2​𝑑s≤|∂Ω|​ε2.\mathcal{R}_{\partial\Omega}(u)=\int_{\partial\Omega}\bigl(u(x)-g(x)\bigr)^{2}\,ds\leq\lvert\partial\Omega\rvert\,\varepsilon^{2}.

Finally, for the FK term we use that u⋆u^{\star} is itself the target in (D.3), hence

ℛFK​(u)=𝔼​[|u​(XFK)−u⋆​(XFK)|2]≤∥u−u⋆∥C​(Ω¯)2≤ε2.\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{FK}}(u)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\bigl|u(X^{\mathrm{FK}})-u^{\star}(X^{\mathrm{FK}})\bigr|^{2}\bigr]\leq\lVert u-u^{\star}\rVert_{C(\overline{\Omega})}^{2}\leq\varepsilon^{2}.

Collecting these three bounds and inserting the weights gives (D.19) with a constant CriskC_{\mathrm{risk}} that depends only on the coefficients of ℒ\mathcal{L}, the domain, and the weights. The bound (D.20) then follows from (D.17). ∎

D.3 Optimization Error Bound

We next control the optimization error incurred by terminating gradient descent after a finite number of iterations. Throughout this subsection we fix the sample set and view the empirical FK-PINN loss

ℓ​(𝜽):=ℛ^​(u𝜽)\ell(\bm{\theta}):=\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u_{\bm{\theta}})

as a deterministic function of the parameters.

We rely on the Polyak–Łojasiewicz framework of Karimi et al. (2016); Liu et al. (2022). A function ℓ:ℝP→ℝ\ell:\mathbb{R}^{P}\to\mathbb{R} satisfies a local PL∗ condition on a set S⊂ℝPS\subset\mathbb{R}^{P} with constant μ>0\mu>0 if

ℓ​(𝜽)−ℓ​(𝜽⋆)≤12​μ​∥∇ℓ​(𝜽)∥22,∀𝜽∈S,\ell(\bm{\theta})-\ell(\bm{\theta}^{\star})\leq\frac{1}{2\mu}\,\lVert\nabla\ell(\bm{\theta})\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad\forall\bm{\theta}\in S, (D.21)

for some global minimizer 𝜽⋆∈S\bm{\theta}^{\star}\in S of ℓ\ell. If, in addition, ℓ\ell is β\beta-smooth on SS (that is, ∥∇ℓ​(𝜽)−∇ℓ​(𝜽′)∥2≤β​∥𝜽−𝜽′∥2\lVert\nabla\ell(\bm{\theta})-\nabla\ell(\bm{\theta}^{\prime})\rVert_{2}\leq\beta\lVert\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\rVert_{2} for all 𝜽,𝜽′∈S\bm{\theta},\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\in S), the ratio

κℓ​(S):=βμ\kappa_{\ell}(S):=\frac{\beta}{\mu}

plays the role of a condition number.

The following result is a special case of Liu et al. (2022, Theorem 6).

Theorem D.7 (Gradient descent under a local PL∗ condition).

Let ℓ\ell be differentiable and β\beta-smooth on a convex set S⊂ℝPS\subset\mathbb{R}^{P}, and assume that ℓ\ell satisfies the PL∗ condition (D.21) on SS with constant μ>0\mu>0. Let 𝛉0∈S\bm{\theta}_{0}\in S and consider gradient descent

𝜽t+1=𝜽t−η​∇ℓ​(𝜽t),\bm{\theta}_{t+1}=\bm{\theta}_{t}-\eta\nabla\ell(\bm{\theta}_{t}),

with a fixed step size η∈(0,2/β]\eta\in(0,2/\beta]. Suppose that all iterates remain in SS. Then for all t≥0t\geq 0,

ℓ​(𝜽t)−ℓ​(𝜽⋆)≤(1−η​μ)t​(ℓ​(𝜽0)−ℓ​(𝜽⋆)).\ell(\bm{\theta}_{t})-\ell(\bm{\theta}^{\star})\leq\bigl(1-\eta\mu\bigr)^{t}\bigl(\ell(\bm{\theta}_{0})-\ell(\bm{\theta}^{\star})\bigr). (D.22)

In Theorem 5.4 we proved that the FK-augmented loss enjoys a PL∗ inequality with a condition number that stays uniformly bounded as the number of collocation points increases. We translate this consequence for the empirical loss.

Corollary D.8 (Uniform PL∗ geometry for FK-PINNs).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 5.4 there exist a convex set S⊂ℝPS\subset\mathbb{R}^{P}, constants μFK>0\mu_{\mathrm{FK}}>0, βFK<∞\beta_{\mathrm{FK}}<\infty and an initialization 𝛉0∈S{\bm{\theta}}_{0}\in S such that the empirical loss ℓ​(𝛉)=ℛ^​(u𝛉)\ell(\bm{\theta})=\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u_{\bm{\theta}}) satisfies the PL∗ condition (D.21) on SS with constant μFK\mu_{\mathrm{FK}}, is βFK\beta_{\mathrm{FK}}-smooth on SS, and the associated condition number

κFK:=βFKμFK\kappa_{\mathrm{FK}}:=\frac{\beta_{\mathrm{FK}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{FK}}}

is bounded by a constant that does not depend on (Nint,N∂Ω,NFK)(N_{\mathrm{int}},N_{\partial\Omega},N_{\mathrm{FK}}).

Under Corollary D.8, gradient descent with a suitable step size converges linearly to an empirical minimizer. We quantify the corresponding optimization error in terms of the number of iterations.

Proposition D.9 (Optimization error bound).

Let {𝛉t}t≥0\{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be the gradient descent iterates for ℓ​(𝛉)=ℛ^​(u𝛉)\ell(\bm{\theta})=\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u_{\bm{\theta}}) with step size η∈(0,2/βFK]\eta\in(0,2/\beta_{\mathrm{FK}}], initialized at 𝛉0{\bm{\theta}}_{0} as in Corollary D.8. Let

u^∈arg​minu∈𝒰⁡ℛ^​(u)\widehat{u}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u)

be an empirical minimizer and write 𝛉⋆{\bm{\theta}}^{\star} for a parameter vector with u𝛉⋆=u^u_{{\bm{\theta}}^{\star}}=\widehat{u}. Define the optimization error

ℰopt​(t):=ℛ^​(u𝜽t)−ℛ^​(u^).\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{opt}}(t):=\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}})-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(\widehat{u}). (D.23)

Then, under Corollary D.8, there exist constants Copt,copt>0C_{\mathrm{opt}},c_{\mathrm{opt}}>0 independent of the sample sizes and of tt such that

ℰopt​(t)≤Copt​exp⁡(−copt​t).\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{opt}}(t)\leq C_{\mathrm{opt}}\exp(-c_{\mathrm{opt}}t). (D.24)

In particular, for every t≥0t\geq 0 the network u𝛉tu_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}} is an ℰopt​(t)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{opt}}(t)-approximate empirical minimizer of ℛ^\widehat{\mathcal{R}} in the sense that

ℛ^​(u𝜽t)≤infu∈𝒰ℛ^​(u)+ℰopt​(t).\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u_{{\bm{\theta}}_{t}})\leq\inf_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u)+\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{opt}}(t).
Proof.

Inequality (D.24) follows directly from Theorem D.7 with μ=μFK\mu=\mu_{\mathrm{FK}} and β=βFK\beta=\beta_{\mathrm{FK}}, taking 𝜽⋆{\bm{\theta}}^{\star} to be any parameter vector that realizes an empirical minimizer u^\widehat{u} of ℛ^\widehat{\mathcal{R}}. ∎

D.4 Statistical Error Bound

We now turn to the statistical error ℰstat\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}} in (D.10), which captures the deviation between the population risk and its empirical approximation. Our goal is to obtain non-asymptotic high probability bounds on

ℰstat=supu∈𝒰|ℛ​(u)−ℛ^​(u)|\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}=\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\bigl|\mathcal{R}(u)-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(u)\bigr|

in terms of the number of collocation points and the complexity of the hypothesis class. The analysis follows the now standard Rademacher complexity approach in statistical learning theory, but it has two distinctive features.

First, we operate in a data scarce regime for the FK term: NFKN_{\mathrm{FK}} is allowed to remain bounded while NintN_{\mathrm{int}} and N∂ΩN_{\partial\Omega} grow. Second, we must control the complexity not only of the network outputs u𝜽u_{\bm{\theta}} but also of their first and second order derivatives, since the PDE residual involves ∂αu𝜽\partial^{\alpha}u_{\bm{\theta}} for |α|≤2|\alpha|\leq 2. To the best of our knowledge, existing results of this kind only cover piecewise polynomial activations (see e.g. Jiao et al. (2022); Lu et al. (2022); Lei et al. (2025)), which does not include tanh\tanh. We therefore derive new pseudo-dimension bounds for tanh\tanh networks and their derivatives, building on classical results of Karpinski and Macintyre (1997) and Anthony and Bartlett (2009). These bounds are of independent interest.

D.4.1 Preliminary results

We briefly recall the main tools from empirical process theory that we will use. Detailed expositions can be found, e.g., in Anthony and Bartlett (2009) and Wainwright (2019).

Rademacher complexity.

Let (Zi)i=1n(Z_{i})_{i=1}^{n} be i.i.d. random variables taking values in a space 𝒵\mathcal{Z} and let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a class of measurable functions f:𝒵→ℝf:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}. The empirical Rademacher complexity of ℱ\mathcal{F} with respect to a fixed sample Z1,…,ZnZ_{1},\dots,Z_{n} is

ℜn​(ℱ∣Z1:n):=𝔼σ​[supf∈ℱ1n​∑i=1nσi​f​(Zi)],\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}\mid Z_{1:n}):=\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\Biggl[\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}f(Z_{i})\Biggr],

where (σi)i=1n(\sigma_{i})_{i=1}^{n} are i.i.d. Rademacher variables (ℙ​(σi=1)=ℙ​(σi=−1)=1/2\mathbb{P}(\sigma_{i}=1)=\mathbb{P}(\sigma_{i}=-1)=1/2). The expected Rademacher complexity is ℜn​(ℱ):=𝔼​[ℜn​(ℱ∣Z1:n)]\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}):=\mathbb{E}[\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}\mid Z_{1:n})].

Rademacher complexity controls uniform deviations between empirical and population averages.

Lemma D.10 (Symmetrization and contraction).

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a class of functions f:𝒵→ℝf:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R} with |f​(z)|≤B\lvert f(z)\rvert\leq B for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} and z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}. Then for any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

supf∈ℱ|𝔼​[f​(Z)]−1n​∑i=1nf​(Zi)|≤2​ℜn​(ℱ)+3​B​log⁡(2/δ)2​n.\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\Bigl|\mathbb{E}[f(Z)]-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(Z_{i})\Bigr|\leq 2\,\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F})+3B\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}.

Moreover, if ϕ:ℝ→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is LL-Lipschitz and ϕ​(0)=0\phi(0)=0, then

ℜn​(ϕ∘ℱ)≤L​ℜn​(ℱ),\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\phi\circ\mathcal{F})\leq L\,\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F}),

where ϕ∘ℱ:={ϕ∘f:f∈ℱ}\phi\circ\mathcal{F}:=\{\phi\circ f:f\in\mathcal{F}\}.

A proof of the deviation bound is given in (Wainwright, 2019, Chapter 3). The Lipschitz mapping bound follows from the contraction principle (Ledoux and Talagrand, 2013).

Covering numbers and pseudo-dimension.

Let A⊂ℝnA\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} and consider the metric

d∞​(a,a′):=max1≤i≤n⁡|ai−ai′|.d_{\infty}(a,a^{\prime}):=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\lvert a_{i}-a^{\prime}_{i}\rvert.

An ε\varepsilon-cover of AA with respect to d∞d_{\infty} is a finite subset V⊂ℝnV\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} such that for every a∈Aa\in A there exists v∈Vv\in V with d∞​(a,v)≤εd_{\infty}(a,v)\leq\varepsilon. The covering number 𝒞​(ε,A,d∞)\mathcal{C}(\varepsilon,A,d_{\infty}) is the smallest cardinality of an ε\varepsilon-cover of AA.

Given a function class ℱ\mathcal{F} and a sample Z1:n=(Z1,…,Zn)Z_{1:n}=(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{n}), the evaluation set
