ℱ|Z1:n:={(f​(Z1),…,f​(Zn)):f∈ℱ}⊂ℝn\mathcal{F}|_{Z_{1:n}}:=\bigl\{(f(Z_{1}),\dots,f(Z_{n})):f\in\mathcal{F}\bigr\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}

induces a covering number

𝒞∞​(ε,ℱ,n):=supZ1:n𝒞​(ε,ℱ|Z1:n,d∞).\mathcal{C}_{\infty}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{F},n):=\sup_{Z_{1:n}}\mathcal{C}\bigl(\varepsilon,\mathcal{F}|_{Z_{1:n}},d_{\infty}\bigr).

The pseudo-dimension Pdim​(ℱ)\mathrm{Pdim}(\mathcal{F}) is the standard extension of VC dimension to real-valued function classes (Anthony and Bartlett, 2009). The next two results relate Rademacher complexity, covering numbers and pseudo-dimension.

Lemma D.11 (Dudley’s entropy integral).

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a class of functions f:𝒵→ℝf:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R} with |f|≤B\lvert f\rvert\leq B. Then for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N},

ℜn​(ℱ)≤inf0<δ<B(4​δ+12n​∫δBlog⁡(2​𝒞∞​(ε,ℱ,n))​𝑑ε).\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{F})\leq\inf_{0<\delta<B}\Biggl(4\delta+\frac{12}{\sqrt{n}}\int_{\delta}^{B}\sqrt{\log\bigl(2\,\mathcal{C}_{\infty}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{F},n)\bigr)}\,d\varepsilon\Biggr).
Proposition D.12 (Covering numbers from pseudo-dimension).

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a class of functions from a domain 𝒵\mathcal{Z} to [0,B][0,B] with pseudo-dimension dp:=Pdim​(ℱ)d_{\mathrm{p}}:=\mathrm{Pdim}(\mathcal{F}). Then for every n≥dpn\geq d_{\mathrm{p}} and every ε∈(0,B)\varepsilon\in(0,B),

𝒞∞​(ε,ℱ,n)≤(e​B​nε​dp)dp.\mathcal{C}_{\infty}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{F},n)\leq\biggl(\frac{eBn}{\varepsilon d_{\mathrm{p}}}\biggr)^{d_{\mathrm{p}}}.

Proposition D.12 goes back to Anthony and Bartlett (2009). Combining Lemma D.11 with Proposition D.12 yields Rademacher complexity bounds of order Pdim​(ℱ)/n\sqrt{\mathrm{Pdim}(\mathcal{F})/n} up to logarithmic factors.

D.4.2 Pseudo-dimension bounds for derivatives of tanh\tanh networks

We bound the pseudo-dimension of the classes generated by u𝜽u_{\bm{\theta}} and its first and second order derivatives by proceeding in two steps. First, each derivative Dα​u𝜽D^{\alpha}u_{\bm{\theta}} can be realized by an analytic network that reuses the original weights and biases, at the cost of a controlled increase in the number of computation nodes. Second, we invoke the VC-dimension bound for Pfaffian networks from (Karpinski and Macintyre, 1997), which applies to tanh\tanh since it is an analytic Pfaffian function.

Lemma D.13 (Pseudo-dimension as VC dimension of subgraph thresholds).

Let ℱ⊂{f:X→ℝ}\mathcal{F}\subset\{f:X\to\mathbb{R}\} and define the associated threshold (subgraph) class

thresh⁡(ℱ):={(x,t)↦𝟏​{f​(x)−t>0}:f∈ℱ}⊂{0,1}X×ℝ.\operatorname{thresh}(\mathcal{F}):=\Bigl\{\,(x,t)\mapsto\mathbf{1}\{f(x)-t>0\}\;:\;f\in\mathcal{F}\Bigr\}\subset\{0,1\}^{X\times\mathbb{R}}.

Then

Pdim​(ℱ)=VCdim​(thresh⁡(ℱ)).\mathrm{Pdim}(\mathcal{F})=\mathrm{VCdim}\bigl(\operatorname{thresh}(\mathcal{F})\bigr).
Proof.

The equivalence follows directly from the definitions of pseudo-shattering and shattering after mapping ff to the subgraph threshold map (x,t)↦𝟏​{f​(x)>t}(x,t)\mapsto\mathbf{1}\{f(x)>t\}. A detailed argument is given in (Anthony and Bartlett, 2009, Chapter 11). ∎

We will use the VC-dimension upper bound proved for Pfaffian networks222The notions of Pfaffian networks and the associated complexity parameters (l,N,q,D,dpoly,s)(l,N,q,D,d_{\operatorname{poly}},s) are taken from (Karpinski and Macintyre, 1997). As the required background is quite involved, we refer the reader to said paper for detailed definitions and explanations. in (Karpinski and Macintyre, 1997, Section 4.2). We restate it in the parameterization needed below.

Theorem D.14 (Pseudo-dimension bound via VC bounds for Pfaffian networks (Karpinski and Macintyre, 1997)).

Consider a feedforward Pfaffian network architecture AA in the sense of Karpinski and Macintyre (1997, Section 4.2), with the following complexity parameters:

  • •

    l∈ℕl\in\mathbb{N}: number of trainable real parameters (weights/biases);

  • •

    N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}: number of computation nodes (non-input nodes);

  • •

    dpoly∈ℕd_{\operatorname{poly}}\in\mathbb{N}: an upper bound on the degree of each node polynomial;

  • •

    s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N}: an upper bound on the number of monomials in each node polynomial;

  • •

    q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} and D∈ℕD\in\mathbb{N}: Pfaffian chain length and degree controlling all activation functions used by the architecture (as in Karpinski and Macintyre (1997, Section 4.2)).

Let ℱ​(A)⊂{f:ℝd→ℝ}\mathcal{F}(A)\subset\{f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\} be the resulting real-valued function class computed by AA (as the ll parameters vary freely in ℝl\mathbb{R}^{l}).

Define

Ψ​(l,N,q,D,dpoly,s):=l​N​q​(l​N​q−1)+(16+2​log2⁡dpoly+2​log2⁡s)​l+2​(l+2​l​N​q)​log2⁡l+2​(l+2​l​N​q)​log2⁡(dpoly+D).\Psi(l,N,q,D,d_{\operatorname{poly}},s):=lNq(lNq-1)+(16+2\log_{2}d_{\operatorname{poly}}+2\log_{2}s)\,l+2(l+2lNq)\log_{2}l+2(l+2lNq)\log_{2}(d_{\operatorname{poly}}+D).

Then

Pdim​(ℱ​(A))≤Ψ​(l,N+1,q,D,dpoly,s+1).\mathrm{Pdim}\bigl(\mathcal{F}(A)\bigr)\;\leq\;\Psi\bigl(l,\,N+1,\,q,\,D,\,d_{\operatorname{poly}},\,s+1\bigr).
Proof.

By Lemma D.13,

Pdim​(ℱ​(A))=VCdim​(thresh⁡(ℱ​(A))).\mathrm{Pdim}\bigl(\mathcal{F}(A)\bigr)=\mathrm{VCdim}\bigl(\operatorname{thresh}(\mathcal{F}(A))\bigr).

Now consider the augmented architecture AsubA^{\mathrm{sub}} with one additional input t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} and output gate computing the Boolean predicate

(x,t)↦𝟏​{f​(x)−t>0}, where ​f∈ℱ​(A).(x,t)\mapsto\mathbf{1}\{f(x)-t>0\},\ \text{ where }f\in\mathcal{F}(A).

Concretely, AsubA^{\mathrm{sub}} is obtained by taking the original output polynomial and adding the extra term (−t)(-t). This adds no trainable parameters, increases the number of computation nodes by at most 11 (if the subtraction is implemented as a separate final node), and increases the monomial count bound by at most 11. Thus thresh⁡(ℱ​(A))\operatorname{thresh}(\mathcal{F}(A)) is realized by a Pfaffian network with parameters bounded by (l,N+1,dpoly,s+1,q,D)(l,\,N+1,\,d_{\operatorname{poly}},\,s+1,\,q,\,D).

Applying the VC-dimension upper bound for Pfaffian networks from Karpinski and Macintyre (1997, Section 4.2, end of section) to AsubA^{\mathrm{sub}} yields

VCdim​(thresh⁡(ℱ​(A)))≤Ψ​(l,N+1,q,D,dpoly,s+1),\mathrm{VCdim}\bigl(\operatorname{thresh}(\mathcal{F}(A))\bigr)\leq\Psi\bigl(l,\,N+1,\,q,\,D,\,d_{\operatorname{poly}},\,s+1\bigr),

and the result follows. ∎

Corollary D.15 (Implication of Theorem D.14 for fixed activations).

Assume q,D,dpolyq,D,d_{\operatorname{poly}} are absolute constants and s≤poly​(N)s\leq\mathrm{poly}(N). Then there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that, for all l,N≥2l,N\geq 2,

Pdim​(ℱ​(A))≤C​(l​N)2​log⁡(l​N).\mathrm{Pdim}\bigl(\mathcal{F}(A)\bigr)\leq C\,(lN)^{2}\log(lN).

We next need a lemma on the representation of products with analytic networks.

Lemma D.16.

Let φsq​(t)=t2\varphi_{\mathrm{sq}}(t)=t^{2}. In a feedforward architecture allowing tanh\tanh and φsq\varphi_{\mathrm{sq}} hidden units and a linear output, there exists a fixed constant-size subnetwork that maps two scalar inputs (a,b)∈ℝ2(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} to the product a​bab exactly.

Proof.

The identity a​b=12​((a+b)2−a2−b2)ab=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl((a+b)^{2}-a^{2}-b^{2}\bigr) expresses multiplication using one addition, three squaring operations, and one final affine combination. These operations can be implemented by a constant number of units with fixed coefficients, independent of the surrounding network. ∎

The next lemma shows that derivatives of u𝜽u_{\bm{\theta}} with respect to the input variables can be represented by analytic networks with the same depth and with at most a constant factor more parameters.

Lemma D.17.

Fix an architecture (mℓ)ℓ=0L(m_{\ell})_{\ell=0}^{L} with m0=dm_{0}=d and mL=1m_{L}=1, and write

P:=∑ℓ=1L(mℓ​mℓ−1+mℓ),Nhid:=∑ℓ=1L−1mℓ.P:=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}(m_{\ell}m_{\ell-1}+m_{\ell}),\ \ N_{\mathrm{hid}}:=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L-1}m_{\ell}.

Let uθu_{\theta} be the corresponding fully connected tanh\tanh network (with linear output) on Ω\Omega.

For every multi-index α∈ℕ0d\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{d} with 1≤|α|≤21\leq|\alpha|\leq 2, there exists a feedforward Pfaffian network architecture AαA_{\alpha} (in the sense of Karpinski and Macintyre (1997, Section 4.2)) with the following properties:

  1. 1.

    (Parameter sharing) The set of trainable parameters of AαA_{\alpha} is exactly the original parameter vector θ∈ℝP\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{P} (no additional free parameters).

  2. 2.

    (Exact derivative) For every θ\theta and every x∈Ωx\in\Omega,

    Aα​(x;θ)=Dα​uθ​(x).A_{\alpha}(x;\theta)=D^{\alpha}u_{\theta}(x).
  3. 3.

    (Computation nodes) The number NαN_{\alpha} of computation nodes of AαA_{\alpha} satisfies

    Nα≤Cd,|α|​Nhid+3,N_{\alpha}\leq C_{d,|\alpha|}\,N_{\mathrm{hid}}+3,

    where one may take

    Cd,1:=3+5​d,Cd,2:=8+5​d+132​d​(d+1).C_{d,1}:=3+5d,\ \ C_{d,2}:=8+5d+\frac{13}{2}d(d+1).
Proof.

Write the base tanh\tanh network as a feedforward computation graph with affine maps, tanh\tanh nonlinearities, and a final linear output. This fits the Pfaffian network framework of (Karpinski and Macintyre, 1997) because affine maps are polynomials and tanh\tanh is Pfaffian.

Fix a hidden neuron with pre-activation aa and activation z=tanh⁡(a)z=\tanh(a). Using only tanh\tanh, squaring, affine combinations, and the exact multiplication subnetwork from Lemma D.16, we can compute z2z^{2}, s:=1−z2s:=1-z^{2}, and t:=−2​z+2​z3t:=-2z+2z^{3}. The identities tanh′⁡(a)=s\tanh^{\prime}(a)=s and tanh′′⁡(a)=t\tanh^{\prime\prime}(a)=t then hold exactly.

We construct AαA_{\alpha} by propagating first and second input derivatives through the graph using the chain rule. For each input coordinate i∈{1,…,d}i\in\{1,\dots,d\}, ∂ia\partial_{i}a is an affine combination of derivatives from the previous layer with coefficients given by the original weights, and ∂iz=s​∂ia\partial_{i}z=s\,\partial_{i}a is obtained using one multiplication subnetwork. Similarly, for 1≤i≤j≤d1\leq i\leq j\leq d, ∂i​ja\partial_{ij}a is affine in previous-layer derivatives and

∂i​jz=t​(∂ia)​(∂ja)+s​∂i​ja\partial_{ij}z=t\,(\partial_{i}a)(\partial_{j}a)+s\,\partial_{ij}a

is implemented using three multiplications and one affine combination. All trainable coefficients are reused from θ\theta, while any additional coefficients introduced by squaring, addition, and the product construction are fixed constants. This gives parameter sharing and the exact derivative identity.

It remains to bound the number of computation nodes. Using the concrete multiplication construction of Lemma D.16, one multiplication can be implemented with a constant number of computation nodes, and we may upper bound this constant by 44. For each hidden neuron, computing zz, z2z^{2}, and s=1−z2s=1-z^{2} costs 33 nodes. For each ii, computing ∂ia\partial_{i}a costs one affine node and computing ∂iz=s​∂ia\partial_{i}z=s\,\partial_{i}a costs at most 44 nodes, for a total of 5​d5d nodes. For second derivatives, computing z3z^{3} and t=−2​z+2​z3t=-2z+2z^{3} costs at most 55 additional nodes. For each pair 1≤i≤j≤d1\leq i\leq j\leq d, the update for ∂i​jz\partial_{ij}z uses one affine node for ∂i​ja\partial_{ij}a and at most 33 multiplications, hence at most 1+3⋅4=131+3\cdot 4=13 nodes per pair. Since there are d​(d+1)/2d(d+1)/2 such pairs, the per-neuron cost is bounded by Cd,1=3+5​dC_{d,1}=3+5d for first derivatives and by Cd,2=8+5​d+132​d​(d+1)C_{d,2}=8+5d+\tfrac{13}{2}d(d+1) for derivatives up to order 22. Multiplying by NhidN_{\mathrm{hid}} and adding a constant number of output nodes yields the claimed bound on NαN_{\alpha}. ∎

We now define, for k∈{0,1,2}k\in\{0,1,2\}, the derivative classes

ℱ(k):={Dα​u𝜽:u𝜽∈𝒰L,m,B,α∈ℕ0d,|α|=k},\mathcal{F}^{(k)}:=\Bigl\{D^{\alpha}u_{\bm{\theta}}:u_{\bm{\theta}}\in\mathcal{U}_{L,m,B},\ \alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{d},\ |\alpha|=k\Bigr\}, (D.25)

with the convention that D0​u𝜽=u𝜽D^{0}u_{\bm{\theta}}=u_{\bm{\theta}}. Lemma D.17 and Corollary D.15 together give the following quantitative bound.

Proposition D.18 (Pseudo-dimension of tanh\tanh networks and their up-to-order-two derivatives).

Let 𝒰L,m,B\mathcal{U}_{L,m,B} be as in (D.15) with architecture (mℓ)ℓ=0L(m_{\ell})_{\ell=0}^{L}, and define

P:=∑ℓ=1L(mℓ​mℓ−1+mℓ),Nhid:=∑ℓ=1L−1mℓ, and ​Nk:=Cd,k​Nhid+3,P:=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}(m_{\ell}m_{\ell-1}+m_{\ell}),\ \ N_{\mathrm{hid}}:=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L-1}m_{\ell},\ \text{ and }N_{k}:=C_{d,k}\,N_{\mathrm{hid}}+3,

with

Cd,0:=1,Cd,1:=3+5​d, and ​Cd,2:=8+5​d+132​d​(d+1).C_{d,0}:=1,\ \ C_{d,1}:=3+5d,\ \text{ and }C_{d,2}:=8+5d+\frac{13}{2}d(d+1).

Then there exists a constant Cpdim>0C_{\mathrm{pdim}}>0 depending only on dd and on the activation family (ultimately tanh\tanh) such that for each k∈{0,1,2}k\in\{0,1,2\},

Pdim​(ℱ(k))≤Cpdim​(P​Nk)2​log⁡(P​Nk).\mathrm{Pdim}\bigl(\mathcal{F}^{(k)}\bigr)\leq C_{\mathrm{pdim}}\,(PN_{k})^{2}\log(PN_{k}).
Proof.

Fix k∈{0,1,2}k\in\{0,1,2\} and a multi-index α\alpha with |α|=k|\alpha|=k. By Lemma D.17, the class ℱ(α):={Dα​uθ:θ∈ΘL,m}\mathcal{F}^{(\alpha)}:=\{D^{\alpha}u_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{L,m}\} is contained in the Pfaffian network class ℱ​(Aα)\mathcal{F}(A_{\alpha}) of an architecture with l=Pl=P trainable parameters and at most NkN_{k} computation nodes. Hence

Pdim​(ℱ(α))≤Pdim​(ℱ​(Aα)).\mathrm{Pdim}(\mathcal{F}^{(\alpha)})\leq\mathrm{Pdim}(\mathcal{F}(A_{\alpha})).

Applying Corollary D.15 (a consequence of Theorem D.14) gives

Pdim​(ℱ(α))≤C​(P​Nk)2​log⁡(P​Nk)\mathrm{Pdim}(\mathcal{F}^{(\alpha)})\leq C(PN_{k})^{2}\log(PN_{k})

for a constant CC depending only on the fixed activation family.

Finally, ℱ(k)=⋃|α|=kℱ(α)\mathcal{F}^{(k)}=\bigcup_{|\alpha|=k}\mathcal{F}^{(\alpha)} is a finite union over (d+k−1k)\binom{d+k-1}{k} multi-indices. Using the standard finite-union bound for pseudo-dimension (Anthony and Bartlett, 2009, Section 11.2) and absorbing (d+k−1k)\binom{d+k-1}{k} into the constant yields the claim. ∎

Proposition D.18 yields, to the best of our knowledge, the first rigorous bounds for first and second order derivatives of tanh\tanh networks. Together with Lemma D.11 and Proposition D.12, it yields the Rademacher complexity bounds for the PDE, boundary and FK losses stated later in this appendix.

D.4.3 Finite-sample bound on the statistical error

We now bound ℰstat\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}} using the pseudo-dimension estimates from Proposition D.18. Recall that

ℛ​(u)=λPDE​ℛPDE​(u)+λ∂Ω​ℛ∂Ω​(u)+λFK​ℛFK​(u),\mathcal{R}(u)=\lambda_{\mathrm{PDE}}\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{PDE}}(u)+\lambda_{\partial\Omega}\mathcal{R}_{\partial\Omega}(u)+\lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{FK}}(u),

and that ℛ^\widehat{\mathcal{R}} is defined in (D.8). We first separate the contributions of the three components.

Lemma D.19 (Decomposition of the statistical error).

For every hypothesis class 𝒰\mathcal{U},

ℰstat≤λPDE​ℰstatPDE+λ∂Ω​ℰstat∂Ω+λFK​ℰstatFK,\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}\leq\lambda_{\mathrm{PDE}}\,\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}^{\mathrm{PDE}}+\lambda_{\partial\Omega}\,\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}^{\partial\Omega}+\lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}\,\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}^{\mathrm{FK}},

where

ℰstatPDE\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}^{\mathrm{PDE}} :=supu∈𝒰|ℛPDE​(u)−ℛ^PDE​(u)|,\displaystyle:=\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\Bigl|\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{PDE}}(u)-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{PDE}}(u)\Bigr|,
ℰstat∂Ω\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}^{\partial\Omega} :=supu∈𝒰|ℛ∂Ω​(u)−ℛ^∂Ω​(u)|,\displaystyle:=\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\Bigl|\mathcal{R}_{\partial\Omega}(u)-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\partial\Omega}(u)\Bigr|,
ℰstatFK\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}^{\mathrm{FK}} :=supu∈𝒰|ℛFK​(u)−ℛ^FK​(u)|.\displaystyle:=\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\Bigl|\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{FK}}(u)-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{FK}}(u)\Bigr|.
Proof.

This is an immediate consequence of the triangle inequality and the linearity of ℛ\mathcal{R} and ℛ^\widehat{\mathcal{R}} in their three components. ∎

Lemma D.20 (Pseudo-dimension and fixed multipliers / finite sums).

Let ℱ⊂{f:𝒵→ℝ}\mathcal{F}\subset\{f:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}\} be a function class with Pdim​(ℱ)=d<∞\mathrm{Pdim}(\mathcal{F})=d<\infty and let g:𝒵→ℝg:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R} be a fixed (non-random) function. Then

Pdim​(g​ℱ):=Pdim​({z↦g​(z)​f​(z):f∈ℱ})≤d.\mathrm{Pdim}\bigl(g\mathcal{F}\bigr):=\mathrm{Pdim}\bigl(\{z\mapsto g(z)f(z):f\in\mathcal{F}\}\bigr)\leq d.

Moreover, if ℱ1,…,ℱm\mathcal{F}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{F}_{m} are function classes with pseudo-dimensions dj:=Pdim​(ℱj)d_{j}:=\mathrm{Pdim}(\mathcal{F}_{j}), and

ℱsum:={z↦∑j=1mfj​(z):fj∈ℱj},\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{sum}}:=\Bigl\{\,z\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^{m}f_{j}(z)\;:\;f_{j}\in\mathcal{F}_{j}\,\Bigr\},

then there exists a constant Cm>0C_{m}>0, depending only on mm, such that

Pdim​(ℱsum)≤Cm​∑j=1mdj.\mathrm{Pdim}(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{sum}})\leq C_{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}d_{j}.
Proof.

For the first claim, fix a finite sample z1,…,znz_{1},\dots,z_{n} and thresholds r1,…,rn∈ℝr_{1},\dots,r_{n}\in\mathbb{R}. If we replace the class ℱ\mathcal{F} by g​ℱg\mathcal{F}, the sign of g​(zi)​f​(zi)−rig(z_{i})f(z_{i})-r_{i} at each point ziz_{i} is determined by the sign of f​(zi)−ri/g​(zi)f(z_{i})-r_{i}/g(z_{i}) whenever g​(zi)≠0g(z_{i})\neq 0, while points with g​(zi)=0g(z_{i})=0 contribute no additional sign variability. Thus the number of sign patterns achievable by g​ℱg\mathcal{F} on any finite sample is at most the number achievable by ℱ\mathcal{F}, so Pdim​(g​ℱ)≤Pdim​(ℱ)\mathrm{Pdim}(g\mathcal{F})\leq\mathrm{Pdim}(\mathcal{F}).

The bound for finite sums is a special case of the general pseudo-dimension bound for linear combinations of real-valued function classes as shown by Anthony and Bartlett (2009, Chapter 11). Since the number mm of summands is fixed in our setting, its contribution can be absorbed into the constant CmC_{m}. ∎

We treat each term in Lemma D.19 with Lemma D.10 applied to an appropriate function class. We illustrate the argument for ℰstatPDE\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}^{\mathrm{PDE}}; the remaining terms follow in the same way.

Define

ℱPDE:={x↦|Ω|​(ℒ​u​(x)−f​(x))2:u∈𝒰}.\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{PDE}}:=\Bigl\{x\mapsto\lvert\Omega\rvert\,\bigl(\mathcal{L}u(x)-f(x)\bigr)^{2}:u\in\mathcal{U}\Bigr\}.

Define the (unsquared) residual class

𝒢PDE:={x↦ℒ​u​(x)−f​(x):u∈𝒰}.{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{PDE}}:=\Bigl\{x\mapsto\mathcal{L}u(x)-f(x):u\in\mathcal{U}\Bigr\}.

By the bounds above we have

supg∈𝒢PDEsupx∈Ω|g​(x)|≤CPDE.\sup_{g\in{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{PDE}}}\sup_{x\in\Omega}\lvert g(x)\rvert\leq C_{\mathrm{PDE}}.

The mapping u↦ℒ​uu\mapsto\mathcal{L}u is linear in uu and involves only first and second order derivatives. In particular, every g∈𝒢PDEg\in{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathrm{PDE}} can be written as a finite linear combination (with fixed coefficient functions given by the coefficients of ℒ\mathcal{L} and by −f-f) of functions from the derivative classes ℱ(0),ℱ(1),ℱ(2)\mathcal{F}^{(0)},\mathcal{F}^{(1)},\mathcal{F}^{(2)} defined in (D.25). Note that for every g∈𝒢PDEg\in\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{PDE}} the function

≤supu∈𝒰|𝔼​[(u​(XFK)−u⋆​(XFK))2]−1NFK​∑k=1NFK(u​(xkFK)−u⋆​(xkFK))2|\displaystyle\leq\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\Biggl|\mathbb{E}\bigl[(u(X^{\mathrm{FK}})-u^{\star}(X^{\mathrm{FK}}))^{2}\bigr]-\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}\bigl(u(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}})-u^{\star}(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}})\bigr)^{2}\Biggr|
+supu∈𝒰|1NFK​∑k=1NFK[(u​(xkFK)−u⋆​(xkFK))2−(u​(xkFK)−u^MC​(xkFK))2]|\displaystyle\quad+\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\Biggl|\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}\bigl[(u(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}})-u^{\star}(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}}))^{2}-(u(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}})-\widehat{u}^{\mathrm{MC}}(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}}))^{2}\bigr]\Biggr|

supu∈𝒰|1NFK​∑k=1NFK(2​(u​(xkFK)−u⋆​(xkFK))​b​(xkFK)−b​(xkFK)2)|≤4​B​∥b∥L∞​(Ω)+∥b∥L∞​(Ω)2.\sup_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\Biggl|\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}\Bigl(2\,(u(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}})-u^{\star}(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}}))\,b(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}})-b(x_{k}^{\mathrm{FK}})^{2}\Bigr)\Biggr|\leq 4B\,\lVert b\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\lVert b\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}^{2}.

so that ∥b∥L∞​(Ω)≤εbias\lVert b\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{bias}}. We keep the contribution 4​B​εbias+εbias24B\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{bias}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{bias}}^{2} explicit in the final bound.

The remaining stochastic contribution in BFKB_{\mathrm{FK}} involves the mean-zero sub-exponential fluctuations ζk\zeta_{k}. The genuinely stochastic part, involving the ζk\zeta_{k}, is mean-zero and sub-exponential, and a standard Bernstein-type argument yields a contribution of order 𝒪​(NFK−1/2)\mathcal{O}(N_{\mathrm{FK}}^{-1/2}) (up to logarithmic factors), as we show in Appendix C.

Combining these ingredients we obtain the following finite-sample bound on the full statistical error.

+CFK​[(P​N0)​log⁡(P​N0)+log⁡(6/δ)NFK+log⁡(6/δ)NFK+log⁡(6/δ)NFK]+Cbias​(εbias+εbias2),\displaystyle\quad+C_{\mathrm{FK}}\Biggl[(PN_{0})\sqrt{\frac{\log(PN_{0})+\log(6/\delta)}{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}}+\sqrt{\frac{\log(6/\delta)}{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}}+\frac{\log(6/\delta)}{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}\Biggr]+C_{\mathrm{bias}}\bigl(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{bias}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{bias}}^{2}\bigr), (D.27)

where εbias:=Cbias​Δ​t+CT​e−κ​Tmax\varepsilon_{\mathrm{bias}}:=C_{\mathrm{bias}}\sqrt{\Delta t}+C_{T}e^{-\kappa T_{\max}} is the FK Monte Carlo bias level from Proposition 6.1. In particular, for fixed network size PP and fixed confidence level, the first bracket in (D.27) tends to zero as Nint,N∂Ω→∞N_{\mathrm{int}},N_{\partial\Omega}\to\infty, while the second bracket decays only as NFK−1/2N_{\mathrm{FK}}^{-1/2} (up to logarithmic factors). Thus, when NFKN_{\mathrm{FK}} is small or remains bounded, the FK contribution controls the asymptotic order of ℰstat\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}} and induces a nonvanishing statistical floor of order

ℰstat≳(P​N2)​log⁡(P​N2)NFK.\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}\gtrsim(PN_{2})\sqrt{\frac{\log(PN_{2})}{N_{\mathrm{FK}}}}.

The dependence on log⁡(6/δ)\log(6/\delta) in (D.27) comes from a simple union bound. We first apply Lemma D.21 to control ℰstatPDE\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}^{\mathrm{PDE}} with failure probability at most δ/3\delta/3 by replacing log⁡(2/δ)\log(2/\delta) there with log⁡(6/δ)\log(6/\delta). The same argument applied to the boundary term ℰstat∂Ω\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}^{\partial\Omega} yields an analogous bound, again with failure probability at most δ/3\delta/3. Finally, the FK contribution ℰstatFK\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{stat}}^{\mathrm{FK}} is controlled in the same way, with its own failure probability bounded by δ/3\delta/3 and with the same replacement of log⁡(2/δ)\log(2/\delta) by log⁡(6/δ)\log(6/\delta). A union bound over these three events shows that, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, all three component bounds hold simultaneously, which implies (D.27) via Lemma D.19.

D.5 Putting it all together: non-asymptotic error bounds for FK-PINNs

We are now ready to combine the approximation, statistical and optimization bounds to prove the non-asymptotic error estimate announced in Theorem 6.2.

Corollary D.25 shows that, if the number of FK trajectories NFKN_{\mathrm{FK}} were allowed to grow, a depth-33 FK-PINN with optimally chosen width would achieve the rate NFK−(s−2)/(2​d+4​(s−2))N_{\mathrm{FK}}^{-(s-2)/(2d+4(s-2))} up to logarithmic factors. This matches the asymptotic behaviour proved by Doumèche et al. (2025) for PINNs with dense physics sampling: in that ideal regime, FK supervision does not worsen the leading statistical exponent.

Our focus, however, is the genuinely sparse FK regime, where NFKN_{\mathrm{FK}} is fixed while NintN_{\mathrm{int}} and N∂ΩN_{\partial\Omega} may grow. In this setting the FK term behaves as an irreducible noise floor: even as Nint,N∂Ω→∞N_{\mathrm{int}},N_{\partial\Omega}\to\infty and T→∞T\to\infty, the excess risk cannot be made uniformly small, because it is pinned down by the few noisy FK labels. This loss of uniform guarantees for the excess risk is the real “price” of FK supervision. We accept it in exchange for the PL∗ geometry and uniform conditioning provided by the FK term (Corollary D.8), which yield fast optimization (Proposition D.9). How to exploit a fixed FK budget (placement of FK points, choice of λFK\lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}, etc.) so as to mitigate this statistical saturation while retaining the optimization benefits is an interesting avenue for future work.

Appendix E Numerical Experiments

We now illustrate our theoretical results by a series of numerical experiments.

E.1 Equations Considered

We begin by specifying the concrete equations used to benchmark the proposed FK-PINNs framework. As discussed earlier, our focus is on regimes where traditional PINNs often become inaccurate or unstable, due to difficulties such multiscale coupling, singular perturbations, high frequencies etc. in the PDE data, leading to extremely stiff loss landscapes. Besides the Schrödinger equation introduced in the main text, we also consider the three following representative classes of problems:

E.1.1 Poisson Equation

We consider a prototypical elliptic bounded value problem on a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} with boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega:

−Δ​u​(x)=f​(x)x∈Ω,-\Delta u(x)=f(x)\qquad x\in\Omega, (E.1)

with Dirichlet boundary conditions

u​(x)=g​(x)x∈∂Ω.u(x)=g(x)\qquad x\in\partial\Omega.

Here u​(x)u(x) denotes the stationary potential or steady-state field generated by a source term f​(x)f(x). In multiscale settings, f​(x)f(x) and/or the solution u​(x)u(x) can exhibit sharp layers and small-scale structures, which pose challenges for standard PINNs due to spectral bias.

E.1.2 Mean Escape Time

Consider an overdamped diffusion process in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d},

d​Xt=b​(Xt)​d​t+σ​(Xt)​d​Wt,\mathrm{d}X_{t}=b(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}W_{t}, (E.2)

and a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} with boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega. The mean first exit time (or mean escape time) τ​(x)\tau(x) from Ω\Omega solves the elliptic PDE

ℒ​τ​(x)=−1,x∈Ω,\mathcal{L}\,\tau(x)=-1,\qquad x\in\Omega, (E.3)

with boundary condition

τ​(x)=0,x∈∂Ω,\tau(x)=0,\qquad x\in\partial\Omega,

where ℒ\mathcal{L} is the infinitesimal generator

ℒ​ϕ=−∇V⋅∇ϕ+β−1​Δ​ϕ\mathcal{L}\phi=-\nabla V\cdot\nabla\phi+\beta^{-1}\Delta\phi (E.4)

where β\beta is inverse temperature. The function τ​(x)\tau(x) quantifies how long, on average, trajectories starting from xx remain inside Ω\Omega. In metastable or small-noise regimes, τ​(x)\tau(x) can vary over exponentially large scales, leading to stiff elliptic problems characterized by sharp boundary layers and high-contrast magnitudes that are challenging for standard PINNs.

E.1.3 Committor Function

For the same diffusion process

d​Xt=b​(Xt)​d​t+σ​(Xt)​d​Wt,\mathrm{d}X_{t}=b(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}W_{t}, (E.5)

let A,B⊂ℝdA,B\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be two disjoint sets, and define Ω=ℝd∖(A∪B)\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus(A\cup B). The committor function q​(x)q(x) is the probability that a trajectory starting at xx reaches BB before AA. It is characterized as the solution of the elliptic boundary value problem

ℒ​q​(x)=0x∈Ω,\mathcal{L}\,q(x)=0\ \ \ \ \ x\in\Omega, (E.6)

with boundary conditions

q​(x)=0x∈A,q​(x)=1x∈B,q(x)=0\ \ \ \ x\in A,\ \ \ \ \ \ \ q(x)=1\ \ \ \ x\in B,

where ℒ\mathcal{L} is the same generator as above. The committor encodes the effective reaction coordinate in transition path theory and large deviation theory, typically exhibiting sharp interfaces between metastable basins. Such boundary layers and rare-event structures are difficult to resolve with conventional PINNs, especially under small-noise conditions.

E.2 Evaluation of FK-PINNs against baseline PINNs

In this section, we evaluate our proposed FK-PINNs by testing them on the aforementioned PDEs, and comparing how they perform against standard PINNs as baseline. This choice is to isolate the effect of the Feynman-Kac supervision terms on the training dynamics.

E.2.1 Implementation details

Neural Network Architectures. All neural networks (baseline and FK-PINNs) used for these experiments are fully connected tanh\tanh networks with 4 hidden layers, and 128 neurons per layer.

Training Schedule. All neural networks (baseline and FK-PINNs) used for these experiments are trained using the Adam optimizer for 30,00030,000 iterations, followed by 15,00015,000 iterations of L-BFGS to fine-tune the solution. For the Adam phase, we implement a step-based exponential decay schedule, where the initial learning rate of 10−310^{-3} is decayed every kk iterations by a factor of γ=exp⁡(ln⁡(10−3)/(N/k))\gamma=\exp(\ln(10^{-3})/(N/k)), reaching a final learning rate of 10−610^{-6}.

Feynman-Kac data supervision. To generate the FK “data points”, we use Algorithm 1 and set Δ​t=10−3\Delta t=10^{-3}, NMC=500N_{\mathrm{MC}}=500, and Tmax=∞T_{\max}=\infty (we simulate the trajectories until escape). As for the number of FK points, we first choose a number NcollN_{\mathrm{coll}} of collocation points, and fix a proportion pdata∈(0,1)p_{\mathrm{data}}\in(0,1) of randomly selected points for which we compute the FK label. We thus define

NFK:=⌊pdata​Ncoll⌋,Nint:=Ncoll−NFK.N_{\mathrm{FK}}:=\big\lfloor p_{\mathrm{data}}\,N_{\mathrm{coll}}\big\rfloor,\quad N_{\mathrm{int}}:=N_{\mathrm{coll}}-N_{\mathrm{FK}}. (E.7)

We fix pdata=0.02p_{\mathrm{data}}=0.02 for all experiments in E.2. We will further explore the effects of different NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}}, Δ​t\Delta t, and pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} on the experimental results in E.5.

Metrics. To evaluate the performance of the models, we use the L2L^{2} and H1H^{1} error metrics in both absolute and relative forms.

L2L^{2} absolute error: Labs2​(fθ)=1N​∑n=1N|fθ​(xn)−uref​(xn)|2\displaystyle L_{\text{abs}}^{2}(f_{\theta})=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left|f_{\theta}(x_{n})-u_{\text{ref}}(x_{n})\right|^{2}} (E.8)
L2L^{2} relative error: Lrel2​(fθ)=1N​∑n=1N|fθ​(xn)−uref​(xn)|21N​∑n=1N|uref​(xn)|2\displaystyle L_{\text{rel}}^{2}(f_{\theta})=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left|f_{\theta}(x_{n})-u_{\text{ref}}(x_{n})\right|^{2}}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left|u_{\text{ref}}(x_{n})\right|^{2}}} (E.9)
H1H^{1} absolute error: Habs1​(fθ)=1N​∑n=1N|fθ​(xn)−uref​(xn)|2+‖∇fθ​(x)−∇uref​(x)‖2\displaystyle H_{\text{abs}}^{1}(f_{\theta})=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left|f_{\theta}(x_{n})-u_{\text{ref}}(x_{n})\right|^{2}+\left\|\nabla f_{\theta}(x)-\nabla u_{\text{ref}}(x)\right\|^{2}} (E.10)
H1H^{1} relative error: Hrel1​(fθ)=1N​∑n=1N|fθ​(xn)−uref​(xn)|2+‖∇fθ​(x)−∇uref​(x)‖21N​∑n=1N|uref​(xn)|2+‖∇uref​(x)‖2\displaystyle H_{\text{rel}}^{1}(f_{\theta})=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left|f_{\theta}(x_{n})-u_{\text{ref}}(x_{n})\right|^{2}+\left\|\nabla f_{\theta}(x)-\nabla u_{\text{ref}}(x)\right\|^{2}}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left|u_{\text{ref}}(x_{n})\right|^{2}+\left\|\nabla u_{\text{ref}}(x)\right\|^{2}}} (E.11)

E.2.2 Poisson Equation

In this example, we solve the Poisson equation on the square Ω=[0,1]×[0,1]\Omega=[0,1]\times[0,1], with source term given by

f​(x1,x2)=π2​[51​sin⁡(π​x1)​sin⁡(4​π​x2)+156​sin⁡(5​π​x1)​sin⁡(π​x2)+24​sin⁡(2​π​x1)​sin⁡(2​π​x2)+244​sin⁡(5​π​x1)​sin⁡(6​π​x2)],f(x_{1},x_{2})=\pi^{2}[51\sin(\pi x_{1})\sin(4\pi x_{2})+156\sin(5\pi x_{1})\sin(\pi x_{2})+24\sin(2\pi x_{1})\sin(2\pi x_{2})+244\sin(5\pi x_{1})\sin(6\pi x_{2})],

And exact solution u∗u^{*}:

u∗​(x1,x2)=3​sin⁡(π​x1)​sin⁡(4​π​x2)+6​sin⁡(5​π​x1)​sin⁡(π​x2)+3​sin⁡(2​π​x1)​sin⁡(2​π​x2)+4​sin⁡(5​π​x1)​sin⁡(6​π​x2).u^{*}(x_{1},x_{2})=3\sin(\pi x_{1})\sin(4\pi x_{2})+6\sin(5\pi x_{1})\sin(\pi x_{2})+3\sin(2\pi x_{1})\sin(2\pi x_{2})+4\sin(5\pi x_{1})\sin(6\pi x_{2}). (E.12)

We set Ncoll=10000N_{\mathrm{coll}}=10000 interior collocation points, and (Nbc=400N_{\mathrm{bc}}=400) boundary collocation points.

Figure 4 compares the performance of PINNs and FK-PINNs on this Poisson problem with high-frequency oscillations. While both models capture the global solution profile, PINNs exhibit significant absolute errors (up to 9.0), particularly near the oscillatory peaks and boundaries. In contrast, by leveraging the “extra data”, FK-PINNs effectively mitigate spectral bias, achieving a much finer reconstruction with absolute errors nearly an order of magnitude lower.

Figure 5 likewise demonstrates that FK-PINNs achieve superior convergence stability and a significantly lower PDE loss compared to standard PINNs, effectively mitigating the optimization stagnation observed in the vanilla baseline.

E.2.3 Mean Escape Time

We set the domain Ω\Omega as the regular hexagon centered at the origin with circumradius R=2R=2. We set VV as a double-well potential function:

V​(x1,x2)=14​(x12−1)2+α2​x22,V\left(x_{1},x_{2}\right)=\frac{1}{4}(x_{1}^{2}-1)^{2}+\frac{\alpha}{2}x_{2}^{2}, (E.13)

where α=1\alpha=1. The corresponding Mean Escape Time PDE is then given by:

−∇V⋅∇τ+β−1​Δ​τ=−1,-\nabla V\cdot\nabla\tau+\beta^{-1}\Delta\tau=-1, (E.14)

with inverse temperature β=5\beta=5 and zero Dirichlet boundary condition.

Figure 6 shows the solutions learned both by PINNs and FK-PINNs. We see that PINNs (Cols. 2–3) exhibit catastrophic failure on this task, and completely fail to produce a meaningful solution. FK-PINNs (Cols. 4–5), on the other hand, successfully learn the solution and manage to capture the transition layers near the boundary, despite the corner singularities.

The training loss evolutions in Figure 7 reveal that standard PINNs encounter significant optimization stagnation after the initial phase, seemingly getting stuck around a spurious local minimum for the PDE loss. We see on the other hand that FK-PINNs manage to break through the poorly conditioned loss landscape and converge to the true solution.

E.2.4 Committor Function

We now report the performance of FK-PINNs on the committor function problem on the domain Ω=[−1.5,1.2]×[−0.2,2]\Omega=[-1.5,1.2]\times[-0.2,2] with Müller-Brown potential, which is a standard benchmark in transition path studies (E and Vanden-Eijnden, 2006; Vanden-Eijnden and others, 2010). It is defined as the sum of four exponentials:

V​(x,y)=∑k=14Ak​exp⁡[ak​(x−xk0)2+bk​(x−xk0)​(y−yk0)+ck​(y−yk0)2]V(x,y)=\sum_{k=1}^{4}A_{k}\exp\left[a_{k}(x-x_{k}^{0})^{2}+b_{k}(x-x_{k}^{0})(y-y_{k}^{0})+c_{k}(y-y_{k}^{0})^{2}\right] (E.15)

The specific coefficients used to define the potential energy surface in this work are provided in Table 3. These parameters ensure the presence of the characteristic “three-well” structure often used to benchmark transition path sampling and committor function approximations.

We further define two metastable states, AA and BB, which correspond to the reactant and product regions, respectively. These states are represented as circular boundary regions Ω¯A\bar{\Omega}_{A} and Ω¯B\bar{\Omega}_{B} with a fixed radius of r=0.2r=0.2. The centers of these disks, 𝐜A\mathbf{c}_{A} and 𝐜B\mathbf{c}_{B}, are positioned at the primary local minima of the potential:

  • •

    State AA (Reactant): 𝐜A=(−0.5582,1.4417)\mathbf{c}_{A}=(-0.5582,1.4417), satisfying the boundary condition q​(𝐱)=0q(\mathbf{x})=0.

  • •

    State BB (Product): 𝐜B=(0.6235,0.0281)\mathbf{c}_{B}=(0.6235,0.0281), satisfying the boundary condition q​(𝐱)=1q(\mathbf{x})=1.

The domain for the committor equation is thus defined as Ω′:=Ω∖(Ω¯A∪Ω¯B)\Omega^{\prime}:=\Omega\setminus(\bar{\Omega}_{A}\cup\bar{\Omega}_{B})

As highlighted in Figure 8, the PINN solution fails to meaningfully capture the transition regions and the dynamics induced by the loss landscape, unlike FK-PINNs which recover a fully satisfactory solution. The improved training dynamics are also apparent in Figure 9.

E.3 FK supervision improves the loss landscape

We now collect both qualitative and quantitative evidence supporting the improvement of the loss landscape as predicted by Theorem 5.4.

E.3.1 Hessian Condition Number

To provide quantitative justification for the superior convergence of FK-Enhanced PINNs, we analyze the local curvature of the loss landscape near a minimizer through the lens of the empirical Hessian matrix, H=∇θ2ℒ​(θ)H=\nabla^{2}_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta). As discussed in Section 5, the conditioning of the Hessian governs the stability and speed of gradient-based optimization.

The evolution of the Hessian condition number as the number of collocation points increases plotted in Figure 10, suggests, as predicted by Theorem 5.3, that for the standard PINN, the condition number grows polynomially fast with sampling density. The condition number of FK-PINNs however, does not appear to follow such a growth rate, and remains for most sample sizes orders of magnitude below that of the standard PINN, in accordance with Theorem 5.4.

E.3.2 Visualizing the Loss Landscape Geometry

We now turn to a more qualitative understanding of the training difficulty for standard PINNs and FK-PINNs. To do so, we decide to directly visualize the loss landscape itself around a minimizer, by projecting the loss onto a 2D parameter subspace, and visually observe the result (Li et al., 2018; Krishnapriyan et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2024). The resulting landscapes for the Mean Escape Time PDE, as seen in Figure 11, confirm what the theory and the other numerical results so far suggest: the PINN loss landscape exhibits a highly non-convex, jagged geometry, with many oscillations. This explains the failure of PINNs on this challenging PDE. On the other hand, the loss landscape of FK-PINNs appears much more regular and smooth, with a unique, well localized minimizer. This thus provides a vivid illustration of our theory.

E.4 Comparison with other operator preconditioning techniques

Now that the improvements of FK-PINNs over the baseline PINNs is clear, we compare the FK-PINNs with two other “pre-conditioning inspired” approaches to train them. The first one we consider is the Energy Natural Gradient Descent algorithm (ENGD), proposed by Müller and Zeinhofer (2023), and which consists in performing gradient descent in the function space induced by the PDE. The second one is the NysNewtown-Conjugate Gradient Descent Algorithm (NNCG), proposed by Rathore et al. (2024), and which we run after Adam and L-BFGS, as the authors of said paper do to save computational cost.

As per the results reported in Figure 12 and Table 5, the other methods can not handle the stiff loss landscape of the Mean Escape Time PDE and fail just as much as the standard PINN does, despite their non-negligible computational overhead.

E.5 Influence of the Monte Carlo budget

Finally, we report how the “Monte Carlo budget”, i.e., the number NFKN_{\mathrm{FK}} of FK data points we allow ourselves to use relative to the number of collocation points, the number NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}} of paths we use to compute the Monte Carlo average, and the timestep Δ​t\Delta t we use to discretize the SDE influence the performance of FK-PINNs. We take Tmax=∞T_{\max}=\infty in all of the experiments presented below.

As shown in Figure 13, and as one could expect, too coarse discretization Δ​t\Delta t of the SDE leads to solutions which perform worse than the baseline PINN, which could be explained by the large amount of noise in the labels shifting the objective away from the true PDE solution. However we observe clear solution improvement for any discretization finer than Δ​t=10−3\Delta t=10^{-3}, which is well within the standard discretization sizes used to simulate SDE solutions. We likewise observe that for Δ​t=10−3\Delta t=10^{-3}, as even as little as NMC=300N_{\mathrm{MC}}=300 provides clear improvement over the baseline, suggesting that even modest Monte Carlo computational budgets are already sufficient to “lift” the poorly conditioned PINN landscape with our method.

We finally show in Table 6 how the proportion pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} of points used as FK supervision influences the solution quality. Perhaps contrary as to what one would expect, we find that, for the Mean Escape Time at least, there are diminishing returns when adding FK supervision data: while the solution quality improves as pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} slowly increases from zero, we quickly find that there is a threshold where there is no clear improvement in the solution quality, while the time needed to simulate all the NMC×NFKN_{\mathrm{MC}}\times N_{\mathrm{FK}} paths until escape becomes prohibitively large, as the mean escape time is by design costly to estimate by Monte Carlo averages.

These observations suggest that it would be sensible, depending on the PDE being solved, to first fix Δ​t\Delta t, and then preemptively simulate some Euler-Maruyama trajectories of the underlying stochastic process XtX_{t} until escape, in order to estimate roughly the amount of time needed to fully simulate a path. One can then tune pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}, NMCN_{\mathrm{MC}}, and possibly TmaxT_{\max} according to both the time and computational budget one has at disposition.
